sections.body:
The diagnosis of HF requires integrating symptoms, signs, biomarkers, and imaging. No single test confirms or excludes HF — but knowing how each piece contributes lets you build a watertight diagnosis efficiently.

## The ESC diagnostic algorithm

The 2021 ESC HF guidelines recommend a structured diagnostic approach for suspected HF in a non-acute setting:

1. Clinical assessment: symptoms and signs of HF (see Chapter 3)
2. 12-lead ECG: looking for evidence of a cause (LBBB, LVH, Q waves from prior MI, AF) and arrhythmia. A completely normal ECG makes HF unlikely (negative predictive value ~97%). Any abnormality warrants echo.
3. Natriuretic peptides (BNP / NT-proBNP): the most important initial biomarker. If normal, HF is very unlikely. If elevated, proceed to echo.
4. Echocardiography: the central diagnostic tool. Establishes EF, structural abnormality, cause, and severity.
5. Additional investigations as guided by findings (see below).

## Natriuretic peptides — the gatekeeper test

BNP and NT-proBNP are released by ventricular myocytes in response to wall stress (pressure and volume overload). They are the most sensitive biomarkers for HF and are used to both diagnose and prognosticate.

Test | Rule-out threshold (non-acute) | Rule-in threshold | Notes
BNP | <35 pg/mL → HF unlikely | >100 pg/mL → likely HF | Shorter half-life (~20 min). Lower in obese patients. Higher in renal failure.
NT-proBNP | <125 pg/mL → HF unlikely | >300 pg/mL (acute), age-adjusted non-acute | Age-adjusted thresholds: <50 yr >450, 50–75 yr >900, >75 yr >1800 pg/mL. More stable, longer half-life (~1–2h). More affected by renal failure.

Key concept: A normal BNP/NT-proBNP has a very high negative predictive value for HF — it essentially rules it out in low-to-moderate probability cases
The primary value of natriuretic peptides is exclusion. In a patient with unexplained dyspnoea and a BNP <35 pg/mL, cardiac causes of dyspnoea are very unlikely — investigate for pulmonary causes. However, several conditions cause true HF with falsely low natriuretic peptides: obesity (adipose tissue clears and suppresses NPs — severely obese patients with HF may have normal or mildly elevated BNP despite significant HF), early HF, and flash pulmonary oedema (acute, rapid, the NP has not had time to rise). Conversely, NPs are elevated in many conditions that are not HF: AF, PE, CKD, sepsis, RVH — always interpret in clinical context.

## The ECG in HF

The ECG in HF serves two purposes: confirming a likely cause and identifying treatable contributors:

- LBBB: EF is often significantly underestimated in LBBB. But new LBBB in a patient with HF symptoms = consider ischaemic CMP. LBBB also identifies patients who may benefit from CRT (see Chapter 7).
- Q waves in a coronary territory: suggests ischaemic CMP as the cause — even if the MI is remote, the scar is still there.
- LVH (Sokolow-Lyon, Cornell criteria): suggests hypertensive CMP or HCM as the cause.
- Low voltage + LVH on echo (paradox): think cardiac amyloid (infiltrating amyloid "soaks up" electrical voltage despite increasing wall thickness).
- Sinus tachycardia: compensatory SNS activation in decompensated HF. The faster the HR at rest, the worse the compensation.
- AF: very common in HF (present in 30–40%). May be a cause (tachycardia-mediated CMP) or consequence of HF. Rate and rhythm control decisions are critical (Chapter 11).

## Chest X-ray (CXR) in HF

CXR is not diagnostic but supports and grades HF severity:

Finding | What it means
Cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio >0.5 on PA) | LV or RV enlargement. Sensitive but non-specific — also in pericardial effusion.
Upper lobe diversion | In mild-moderate HF (PCWP 12–18 mmHg), pulmonary venous hypertension preferentially distends upper lobe vessels. The upper lobe vessels appear equal to or larger than lower lobe vessels on erect PA film.
Interstitial oedema (Kerley B lines, peribronchial cuffing) | PCWP 18–25 mmHg. Fluid in the interstitium produces horizontal lines at the lung bases (Kerley B lines — short, horizontal, at the costophrenic angles), and fluid around bronchi appears as peribronchial cuffing.
Alveolar oedema ("bat-wing" pattern) | PCWP >25 mmHg. Fluid fills the alveoli, producing a fluffy bilateral perihilar shadowing ("bat wings"). This is pulmonary oedema requiring urgent treatment.
Pleural effusions | Typically bilateral in biventricular HF. Right-sided in pure left HF. Left-sided in isolation should prompt search for another cause (malignancy, exudate).

## Additional investigations by clinical context

- Bloods: FBC (anaemia worsens HF); U&E + creatinine (electrolyte balance, renal function — critical for GDMT dosing); LFTs (hepatic congestion); TFTs (hypothyroidism causes dilated CMP; hyperthyroidism causes AF); glucose/HbA1c (DM is major HF risk factor); iron studies (iron deficiency — treatable, improves symptoms, Chapter 11)
- Cardiac MRI (CMR): gold standard for myocardial characterisation. LGE identifies: ischaemic scar (subendocardial/transmural), myocarditis (midwall/epicardial), amyloid (global subendocardial), sarcoid (patchy midwall/epicardial), HCM (fibrous replacement). CMR is indicated when echo is inconclusive or a specific cardiomyopathy is suspected.
- Coronary angiography or CT coronary angiogram: to exclude ischaemic CMP as the cause of new HFrEF. Ischaemic HF may benefit from revascularisation if there is viable myocardium. STICH trial: CABG + optimal medical therapy vs medical therapy alone in ischaemic HFrEF — mortality benefit at 10 years for revascularisation.
- Endomyocardial biopsy: rarely needed; reserved for suspected giant-cell myocarditis, eosinophilic myocarditis, haemochromatosis, or acute myocarditis not responding to treatment. Low yield for most dilated CMPs.
- Genetic testing: Consider in: age <50 with unexplained CMP; family history of CMP or SCD; HCM; ARVC; LMNA mutation suspected (AV block + CMP in young patient). Mutations in TTN (titin — most common genetic cause of DCM), LMNA, MYH7, MYBPC3, SCN5A are actionable findings.

Exam tip: BNP is falsely low in obesity — use NT-proBNP in obese HF patients. Adipose tissue expresses natriuretic peptide receptors that clear BNP from the circulation. Severely obese patients with significant HF can have BNP <100 pg/mL. NT-proBNP is less affected by obesity and is more reliable in this population. In exam questions: if a patient is described as obese with symptoms of HF but "BNP is normal," this does not exclude HF — check NT-proBNP and proceed to echo.

Checkpoint: A 55-year-old man presents with 6 weeks of progressive dyspnoea. ECG: LBBB (QRS 148 ms). NT-proBNP: 3400 pg/mL. Echo: EF 25%, dilated LV (LVED 72 mm), no regional wall motion abnormality, moderate functional MR. What is the diagnosis, and what is the most important next investigation to determine the management strategy?
Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) causing HFrEF (EF 25%). Key features: dilated LV (LVED 72 mm, normal <58 mm in men), globally depressed EF without regional wall motion abnormality (suggesting a non-ischaemic cause), functional MR (secondary to LV dilation pulling the mitral leaflets apart — this will improve if EF recovers), LBBB (both a consequence and a marker of severity — associated with dyssynchrony). NT-proBNP markedly elevated confirms significant haemodynamic stress. Most important next investigation: coronary angiography (or CT coronary angiogram in lower-risk patients) to exclude ischaemic CMP. A dilated LV with global dysfunction can be ischaemic (diffuse multivessel disease causing global hypokinesis) or non-ischaemic. The distinction matters: ischaemic HFrEF may benefit from revascularisation (STICH trial). If coronaries are clean → non-ischaemic DCM → consider CMR (to look for myocarditis scar, amyloid, sarcoid, or other infiltrative disease) and genetic testing. Start GDMT regardless of aetiology while investigations proceed.

sections.body:
Echo is the central diagnostic test in HF — it confirms the diagnosis, classifies the subtype, identifies the cause, and guides treatment decisions. This chapter teaches you to interpret the key parameters and understand what each one tells you about the failing heart.

## Ejection fraction — measurement and pitfalls

EF = (EDV − ESV) / EDV × 100. It represents the fraction of end-diastolic volume ejected with each contraction. Normal EF: ≥55% (by Simpson's biplane method, the most reproducible technique).

Measurement methods:

- Simpson's biplane (modified Simpson's rule): traces the LV cavity in two apical views (4-chamber and 2-chamber), calculates LV volumes from cross-sectional areas. Most reproducible, preferred by ESC/ACC/AHA.
- Visual estimation ("eyeballing"): experienced operators can estimate EF ±5–10% visually. Useful for rapid assessment but not for serial monitoring or clinical trials.
- 3D echocardiography: most accurate, least dependent on geometric assumptions, still not universally available.

Key concept: EF is ejection fraction — not contraction fraction. A "normal" EF of 55% means 45% of the blood stays in the LV after each beat
This is a subtle but important point. EF = fraction ejected, not fraction that contracts. Even in a normal heart, 45% of the end-diastolic volume stays in the LV as the residual volume. In HFrEF (EF 25%), only 25% is ejected — 75% remains. The dilated LV with low EF may still eject a normal absolute stroke volume if the LV is large enough: SV = EDV × EF. A dilated LV with EDV 250 mL and EF 30% ejects SV = 75 mL — similar to a normal LV (EDV 140 mL × EF 55% = 77 mL). This is why cardiac output can be maintained at rest in dilated CMP despite low EF — the Frank-Starling compensation (dilation) preserves SV temporarily.

## Diastolic function assessment

Diastolic dysfunction is the hallmark of HFpEF and co-exists with systolic dysfunction in HFrEF. The key parameters:

### Transmitral flow (E and A waves)

- E wave: early passive diastolic filling (mitral valve opens → blood rushes into LV driven by the LV-LA pressure gradient)
- A wave: late diastolic filling from atrial contraction (kick)
- E/A ratio: normally >1 (more early filling than late). In impaired relaxation (Grade I diastolic dysfunction): E/A <1 (reversal — the stiff LV relaxes slowly, reducing early passive filling; atrial kick becomes more important)

### E/e' ratio — the most clinically useful diastolic parameter

- e' (tissue Doppler imaging of the mitral annulus): measures the velocity of the mitral annulus in early diastole — a direct measure of myocardial relaxation speed
- E/e': the ratio of mitral inflow velocity (E) to annular tissue velocity (e'). E/e' correlates with LV filling pressure (PCWP):

Equation: E/e' <8 → normal LV filling pressures | E/e' 8–14 → indeterminate | E/e' >14 → elevated LV filling pressures (PCWP >15 mmHg)

### Diastolic dysfunction grading (ASE 2016)

Grade | Relaxation | Filling pressure | Echo pattern | Clinical correlate
Grade I Impaired relaxation | Abnormal | Normal or mildly elevated | E/A <1, prolonged deceleration time, e' reduced bilaterally | Stage B HFpEF risk. Asymptomatic diastolic dysfunction.
Grade II Pseudonormal | Abnormal | Elevated | E/A 1–2, E/e' 10–14, TR velocity 2.6–2.9 m/s | This pattern "looks" normal on transmitral flow but abnormal tissue Doppler reveals elevated filling pressures. Symptoms on exertion.
Grade III Restrictive filling | Severely abnormal | Markedly elevated | E/A ≥2, short deceleration time <160 ms, E/e' >14 | Severe diastolic HF. Symptoms at rest or minimal exertion. Very poor prognosis (if irreversible).

## Other key echo parameters in HF

### LA volume index (LAVI)

Normal LAVI ≤34 mL/m². Dilated LA (LAVI >34 mL/m²) reflects chronic elevation of LV filling pressures — the LA has enlarged in response to chronically elevated filling pressures, like a chronically overstretched balloon. LAVI is a marker of the chronicity and severity of diastolic dysfunction. Elevated LAVI also predicts AF development.

### TAPSE (Tricuspid Annular Plane Systolic Excursion)

Measures RV longitudinal function. Normal TAPSE ≥17 mm. Reduced TAPSE (<17 mm) indicates RV systolic dysfunction — important in biventricular failure, RV infarction, and pulmonary hypertension. TAPSE is simple, reproducible, and clinically actionable.

### Estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP)

Calculated from peak tricuspid regurgitation (TR) velocity: PASP = 4V²TR + estimated RA pressure. Normal PASP <35 mmHg. Elevated PASP in HFrEF indicates pulmonary venous hypertension (secondary pulmonary hypertension from chronic elevated PCWP). PASP >50 mmHg in HFrEF is a poor prognostic marker and a relevant consideration before cardiac transplant (fixed pulmonary hypertension is a relative contraindication).

### IVC diameter and collapsibility

IVC diameter ≤21 mm with >50% collapse on sniffing → RA pressure ≤5 mmHg (euvolaemic). IVC >21 mm with <50% collapse → RA pressure 10–20 mmHg (raised). Used to estimate RA pressure and guide fluid management in acute HF.

Clinical link: The echo report is a roadmap to management decisions. EF → which GDMT drugs. Diastolic parameters → HFpEF or HFrEF. TAPSE → RV function relevant to transplant eligibility, diuretic response. LAVI → chronicity, AF risk. PASP → vasodilator strategy and transplant considerations. Functional MR or TR → secondary valve disease from LV dilation, decide between repair and aggressive HF treatment. Regional wall motion → ischaemic vs non-ischaemic CMP → guide revascularisation decision. Never treat HF without knowing the echo findings.

Exam tip: The EF pitfall in LBBB: LBBB creates dyssynchrony — the septum moves paradoxically (it contracts early, before the lateral wall). This makes the LV appear to have worse function on visual assessment than it truly has. The measured EF in LBBB is often falsely low by 5–10%. In a patient with new LBBB and apparent HFrEF, begin GDMT — but the "true" EF may be somewhat better than measured, and the patient may be a strong CRT candidate (LBBB is the primary indication for CRT — see Chapter 7). After CRT, some LBBB-associated EF reduction reverses completely (the dyssynchrony was the problem, not the myocardium).

Checkpoint: Echo report: EF 62%, LV dimensions normal, E/A 0.7, e' lateral 6 cm/s, e' medial 5 cm/s, E/e' lateral 14, LAVI 42 mL/m², TAPSE 19 mm, PASP 42 mmHg. The patient has dyspnoea and 2+ ankle oedema. What is the HF classification, and what does the E/e' and LAVI combination tell you about the duration and severity of the diastolic dysfunction?
HFpEF — EF 62% (preserved, ≥50%) with symptoms of HF (dyspnoea, oedema) and elevated filling pressures on echo. The E/e' of 14 is on the upper boundary of "elevated" (ESC criterion ≥15 average, ASE criterion >14) — consistent with elevated LV filling pressures. The E/A ratio of 0.7 (Grade I diastolic dysfunction) shows impaired relaxation with an abnormally reduced e' (normal lateral e' ≥10, medial e' ≥7 — both are reduced here). Crucially, the LAVI of 42 mL/m² (normal ≤34 mL/m²) is dilated — this tells you the elevated filling pressures have been present chronically. The LA does not dilate overnight; it enlarges over months to years of chronic pressure loading. Combined interpretation: this patient has chronic HFpEF driven by a stiff, non-compliant LV (impaired relaxation), elevated filling pressures, and a dilated LA from chronic congestion. The elevated PASP (42 mmHg) confirms secondary pulmonary hypertension from chronic venous hypertension. The normal TAPSE (19 mm) indicates the RV is not yet failing. Management: SGLT2 inhibitor, diuretics for symptom control (Chapter 9).

sections.body:
GDMT is the most evidence-backed drug regimen in all of medicine. Four drug classes given simultaneously — each blocking a different arm of the neurohormonal spiral — produce mortality benefits that are additive and clinically massive. This chapter explains each class from mechanism to trial evidence to clinical implementation.

## Why four pillars simultaneously?

The neurohormonal spiral (Chapter 1) operates through multiple parallel pathways: SNS, RAAS (Ang II arm), RAAS (aldosterone arm), and direct cellular energy/metabolic impairment. Blocking one pathway partially compensates for the others — the surviving pathways upregulate. Only simultaneous multi-pathway blockade produces maximum mortality benefit. The 2021 ESC guidelines now recommend initiating all four classes as early as possible, simultaneously where feasible, rather than sequentially over months.

## Pillar 1 — ACEi / ARB / ARNi (RAAS blockade via Ang II)

### Mechanism

ACE inhibitors block the conversion of Ang I → Ang II → reducing: vasoconstriction (SVR ↓ → afterload ↓), aldosterone release (→ Na/water retention ↓), myocardial fibrosis, and SNS activation. ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers) block Ang II at the AT1 receptor — same haemodynamic effect, avoid bradykinin accumulation (so no ACEi cough). ARNi (sacubitril/valsartan) = neprilysin inhibitor + ARB — see Chapter 1.

### Trial evidence

- CONSENSUS (1987): enalapril vs placebo in severe HF (NYHA IV) — 27% mortality reduction at 1 year
- SOLVD Treatment (1991): enalapril in HFrEF (EF ≤35%) — 16% relative mortality reduction, 26% reduction in HF hospitalisation
- PARADIGM-HF (2014): sacubitril/valsartan vs enalapril — 20% further relative risk reduction in CV death/HF hospitalisation. The trial was stopped early for superiority. ARNi now preferred over ACEi in stable HFrEF as the RAAS component.

### Practical implementation

- Start at low dose: ramipril 1.25–2.5 mg OD, lisinopril 2.5–5 mg OD, sacubitril/valsartan 24/26 mg BD
- Titrate every 2–4 weeks to maximum tolerated dose: ramipril 10 mg OD, lisinopril 20–40 mg OD, sacubitril/valsartan 97/103 mg BD (target dose)
- Monitor: creatinine (ACEi causes reduced GFR by ~10–15% from afferent arteriole dilation — this is expected, not a sign of harm unless creatinine rises >30% from baseline), K⁺ (hyperkalaemia risk with renal impairment), BP
- Contraindications: bilateral renal artery stenosis (ACEi causes irreversible renal failure by blocking the vasoconstrictive Ang II that was maintaining GFR); pregnancy (teratogenic — causes fetal renal dysgenesis); hyperkalaemia >5.5; severe aortic stenosis (fixed outflow obstruction + afterload reduction = haemodynamic collapse)
- Do not use ACEi and ARB together (ONTARGET: dual RAAS blockade increases renal failure and hyperkalaemia without additional CV benefit). Use ACEi alone, ARB alone, or ARNi alone — not combinations.
- Washout before switching to ARNi: stop ACEi for ≥36 hours before starting sacubitril/valsartan — to prevent angioedema from combined neprilysin inhibition (bradykinin accumulation from both ACEi + neprilysin inhibitor).

## Pillar 2 — Beta-blockers (SNS blockade)

### Mechanism

Block β1 receptors → reduce HR and contractility → lower myocardial oxygen demand → reduce toxic noradrenaline signalling → allow β1 receptor upregulation → improve myocyte sensitivity to endogenous catecholamines → EF improves over months (reverse remodelling). The HR reduction is itself protective: slower HR = longer diastolic filling time = better coronary perfusion = less ischaemia.

### Trial evidence

- MERIT-HF (1999): metoprolol succinate vs placebo — 34% relative mortality reduction
- COPERNICUS (2001): carvedilol in severe HFrEF (EF <25%) — 35% mortality reduction even in severe HF
- CIBIS-II (1999): bisoprolol — 34% mortality reduction, trial stopped early

### The three evidence-based beta-blockers

Only three BBs have RCT mortality evidence in HFrEF. Others have not been tested and should not be substituted:

- Carvedilol: α1 + β1 + β2 blocker. The α1 blockade provides additional vasodilation (reduces SVR). Twice daily dosing. Start 3.125 mg BD → target 25 mg BD (50 mg BD if >85 kg).
- Bisoprolol: highly selective β1 blocker. Once daily. Start 1.25 mg OD → target 10 mg OD. Preferred in COPD (most β1-selective).
- Metoprolol succinate (extended release): β1-selective. Once daily. Start 12.5–25 mg OD → target 200 mg OD.

Warning: Never start a beta-blocker during acute decompensated HF — and never abruptly stop it in chronic stable HF. The rule: start BB only when the patient is clinically stable (euvolaemic, not on IV inotropes). Acute HF with congestion = a relative contraindication to initiating BB (negative inotropy will worsen acute decompensation). However, if a patient with chronic HFrEF on BB is admitted with decompensation, continue the BB if possible — abrupt withdrawal is associated with worse outcomes (rebound SNS activation). Reduce the dose if necessary but do not stop entirely unless cardiogenic shock or severe bronchospasm.

## Pillar 3 — Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRA)

### Mechanism

Spironolactone and eplerenone block aldosterone receptors in the: kidney (preventing Na/water retention → diuresis, K⁺ sparing), heart (preventing aldosterone-driven myocardial fibrosis — this is the mortality mechanism, not just diuresis), and vasculature (reducing arterial stiffness).

### Trial evidence

- RALES (1999): spironolactone in severe HFrEF (NYHA III–IV) — 30% relative mortality reduction. Stopped early for striking benefit.
- EMPHASIS-HF (2011): eplerenone in mild HFrEF (NYHA II, EF ≤35%) — 37% relative risk reduction in CV death/HF hospitalisation. Extended indication to NYHA II.
- EPHESUS (2003): eplerenone post-MI with EF ≤40% — 15% mortality reduction (discussed in ACS guide).

### Practical implementation

- Indications: HFrEF (EF ≤35%), NYHA II–IV, already on ACEi/ARNi + BB
- Eplerenone preferred over spironolactone in men (less gynaecomastia — eplerenone is more selective for mineralocorticoid receptor, avoids androgen/progesterone receptor side effects)
- Start: eplerenone 25 mg OD or spironolactone 25 mg OD → titrate to 50 mg OD
- Key monitoring: K⁺ and creatinine at 1 and 4 weeks, then every 3–6 months. Withhold if K⁺ >5.0 mmol/L or creatinine >220 µmol/L (eGFR <30)
- The triple whammy: ACEi + MRA + NSAID = dangerous hyperkalaemia and AKI. Avoid NSAIDs in HF patients on ACEi + MRA.

## Pillar 4 — SGLT2 inhibitors (gliflozins)

### Mechanism

Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors were originally developed as glucose-lowering agents. Their cardiovascular benefits in HF are now understood to involve multiple complementary mechanisms beyond glycaemia:

- Osmotic diuresis and natriuresis: SGLT2 in the proximal renal tubule normally reabsorbs glucose and Na⁺. Inhibiting it → glucose + Na⁺ stay in the tubule → osmotic diuresis → volume reduction
- Reduction in preload and afterload: through natriuresis and osmotic effects
- Direct myocardial effects: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce intracellular Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ overload in failing cardiomyocytes → reduces calcium-triggered apoptosis and arrhythmia. Inhibit NHE1 (Na⁺/H⁺ exchanger 1) in the heart, reducing myocardial cell swelling and death.
- Anti-fibrotic and anti-inflammatory effects: reduce cardiac fibrosis and inflammation
- Erythropoietic effect: increase haematocrit (more RBCs) → improved O₂ delivery
- Ketone body utilisation: SGLT2i induce mild ketonaemia → heart preferentially uses ketone bodies as fuel (more efficient than glucose in failing myocardium)

### Trial evidence

- DAPA-HF (2019): dapagliflozin in HFrEF — 26% relative risk reduction in CV death/HF hospitalisation/worsening HF. Benefit was independent of whether patients had diabetes or not. A landmark moment: the first new mortality-reducing HFrEF drug class in >20 years.
- EMPEROR-Reduced (2020): empagliflozin in HFrEF — 25% relative risk reduction in CV death/HF hospitalisation. Also benefits eGFR (slows renal decline).
- EMPEROR-Preserved (2021) and DELIVER (2022): empagliflozin and dapagliflozin in HFpEF — significant reduction in HF hospitalisation and worsening HF events. First therapies with proven benefit in HFpEF.

### Practical implementation

- Dapagliflozin 10 mg OD or empagliflozin 10 mg OD
- Can be started in patients with eGFR ≥20 mL/min (dapagliflozin) or ≥20 mL/min (empagliflozin) — expanded renal access compared to earlier restrictions
- Not dependent on HbA1c — benefit is in non-diabetics too
- Adverse effects: genital mycotic infections (especially in women — advise genital hygiene), urinary tract infections, DKA (rare in type 2 DM, very rare in HF patients without diabetes — hold during prolonged fasting, surgery, serious illness)

Diagram: GDMT — four pillars, mechanisms, mortality benefits, and target doses (drawing not carried over)

## Other HFrEF drugs

### Diuretics — symptom relief, not mortality benefit

Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide) are the cornerstone of symptom management in HF — they reduce congestion rapidly. But they have no proven mortality benefit and excessive use causes neurohormonal activation (loop diuretics cause RAAS upregulation). Use the lowest effective dose to achieve euvolaemia. Patients may self-adjust dose based on daily weights (patient education is key).

### Ivabradine

If/current (funny current) inhibitor in the SA node — slows HR without any negative inotropy. Indicated when HR remains ≥70 bpm despite maximum tolerated BB (or when BB is contraindicated), and EF ≤35%, in sinus rhythm. SHIFT trial: 18% relative risk reduction in CV death/HF hospitalisation. Use: ivabradine 5 mg BD → 7.5 mg BD.

### Hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrate (H-ISDN)

The combination of a vasodilator (hydralazine — reduces afterload) and a venodilator (ISDN — reduces preload) was the original neurohormonal combination before ACEi. V-HeFT I trial showed mortality benefit over placebo. V-HeFT II: enalapril superior to H-ISDN. Now used primarily when: ACEi, ARB, and ARNi are all contraindicated or not tolerated (e.g., severe bilateral renal artery stenosis, persistent ACEi/ARB-related angioedema). Also indicated as add-on therapy in self-identified Black patients with HFrEF (A-HeFT trial — mortality benefit in African American patients specifically, thought to be related to differences in NO bioavailability).

Exam tip: The absolute combined mortality reduction from all four GDMT pillars is approximately 73% relative risk reduction over placebo. A patient with HFrEF EF 25%, untreated: ~35–40% 5-year mortality. The same patient optimally treated with all four pillars at target doses: mortality approaches that of the general age-matched population. This is not trivial — this is among the largest mortality benefit from any medical intervention in chronic disease. Every delay in GDMT initiation is a delay in saving years of life. The old teaching "start one drug at a time and wait months before adding the next" has been replaced by the 2021 ESC guidance: initiate all four classes simultaneously at low doses as early as possible, then titrate each upward.

Checkpoint: A 65-year-old with HFrEF (EF 28%) is on carvedilol 12.5 mg BD, ramipril 5 mg OD, spironolactone 25 mg OD, and furosemide 40 mg OD. His latest BP is 105/72, HR 62 bpm. K⁺ 4.4, creatinine 110 µmol/L (eGFR 58). His last NT-proBNP was 1800 pg/mL (previously 3200 pg/mL — improving). What change to GDMT should you prioritise at this visit, and why?
This patient is missing Pillar 4 — SGLT2 inhibitor. He is on three of the four evidence-based GDMT pillars (ACEi, BB, MRA) but dapagliflozin or empagliflozin has not been started. This is the highest priority addition: eGFR 58 mL/min is well above the threshold of ≥20 mL/min, so the drug is safe to use. The addition of an SGLT2i will provide further mortality benefit independent of the other three drugs (DAPA-HF showed additive benefit on top of background GDMT). Regarding switching ramipril to sacubitril/valsartan (ARNi): this is also appropriate and should be discussed, particularly given the still-elevated NT-proBNP of 1800 pg/mL and incomplete GDMT — PARADIGM-HF showed additional benefit from ARNi over ACEi. The washout procedure applies (stop ramipril, wait ≥36h, start sacubitril/valsartan 24/26 mg BD). A practical plan: add dapagliflozin 10 mg OD today; plan the switch to ARNi at the next visit in 2–4 weeks. Do not increase carvedilol or spironolactone today (BP already 105, which allows further GDMT additions but suggests caution with further neurohormonal agents that might drop BP more).

sections.body:
When drugs are not enough, devices take over. ICD prevents sudden death, CRT resynchronises the failing heart, and LVAD replaces it. Each has precise indications, and getting those indications wrong — either implanting too early or too late — costs lives.

## Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD)

### The problem it solves

Sudden cardiac death (SCD) from ventricular arrhythmia accounts for ~40–50% of deaths in HFrEF. A severely reduced EF creates arrhythmia substrate: scar from prior MI or fibrosis from CMP forms re-entrant circuits → VT → VF → SCD. The ICD detects and terminates VF within seconds.

### Primary prevention ICD — criteria

Implanting an ICD before any arrhythmia event (primary prevention) is indicated when:

- EF ≤35% despite ≥3 months of optimal GDMT
- NYHA Class II–III (ambulatory — not bed-bound Class IV or imminently terminal)
- Expected meaningful survival >1 year
- Ischaemic CMP: ICD implant ≥40 days post-MI (MADIT-II, SCD-HeFT). Non-ischaemic CMP: ICD also indicated (DANISH trial — trend toward mortality benefit; current ESC IIa recommendation; MADIT-IIIb ongoing).

Key concept: The 90-day rule: never implant a primary prevention ICD within 90 days of diagnosis of HFrEF
GDMT causes reverse remodelling — EF improves over 3–6 months in many patients. An EF of 25% at presentation may become 40–45% with optimal GDMT. If you implant an ICD before GDMT has had time to act, you may be implanting unnecessarily in patients whose EF will recover above the threshold. Always wait ≥3 months of optimal GDMT before reassessing EF for ICD eligibility. Similarly, in acute MI: DINAMIT and IRIS trials — early ICD (<40 days post-MI) did not reduce mortality. The 40-day post-MI exclusion is mandatory.

### Secondary prevention ICD

Implanting after a documented sustained VT or resuscitated VF (secondary prevention) has a lower threshold — the event has already occurred, proving the patient is at risk:

- Any resuscitated VF or haemodynamically unstable VT not caused by a reversible cause (ischaemia within 48h, electrolyte abnormality, drug toxicity) → ICD indicated regardless of EF
- Spontaneous sustained VT with structural heart disease → ICD

## Cardiac resynchronisation therapy (CRT)

### The problem it solves

In HFrEF with LBBB, the left bundle branch conducts slowly or not at all. The LV lateral wall activates late (after the septum), creating mechanical dyssynchrony — parts of the LV contract out of sequence, wasting energy. The septum contracts and rebounds before the lateral wall contracts → inefficient pumping. CRT places a third pacing lead on the lateral LV wall (via the coronary sinus) to simultaneously pace the RV and LV lateral wall → restores coordinated contraction → improves EF, reduces MR, reduces LV volume (reverse remodelling), improves symptoms and survival.

### Primary CRT indications (Class I)

- EF ≤35%
- LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms
- NYHA Class II–IV despite optimal GDMT
- Sinus rhythm (CRT-D preferred if also ICD eligible)

### Class IIa indications

- LBBB with QRS 130–149 ms (less certain benefit)
- Non-LBBB (RBBB, non-specific IVCD) with QRS ≥150 ms (less response than LBBB)
- AF with intrinsic QRS ≥150 ms + EF ≤35% + expected ventricular pacing >40% of time
- Patients with conventional pacing indication (e.g., AVB) who have HFrEF and expected high pacing burden — upgrade to CRT to avoid pacing-induced dyssynchrony

Key concept: LBBB is the single best predictor of CRT response — the wider the QRS, the better the response
CRT response rates are highest in LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms (~70–80% of patients show meaningful EF improvement). The reason: LBBB creates the largest electrical dyssynchrony, so correcting it gives the largest mechanical gain. Non-LBBB (RBBB, IVCD) has dyssynchrony from different mechanisms that are less reliably corrected by biventricular pacing. In a patient with EF 28%, LBBB QRS 168 ms, NYHA III — CRT-D (resynchronisation + defibrillator combined) is the single most impactful intervention available. CARE-HF trial: CRT alone ↓ mortality 36%; COMPANION: CRT-D even better. These benefits are on top of GDMT.

### CRT-D vs CRT-P

- CRT-D: CRT + defibrillator (both resynchronisation and arrhythmia protection). Preferred in patients who also meet ICD criteria (most HFrEF patients with EF ≤35%)
- CRT-P: CRT alone (no defibrillator). Consider in: very elderly patients where ICD benefit is less clear, NYHA Class IV patients not transplant/LVAD candidates (where ICD prolongs dying rather than saving life), patients who decline ICD component

### His bundle pacing and left bundle branch area pacing (LBBAP)

Emerging alternatives to conventional CRT for selected patients. His bundle pacing delivers impulses at the His bundle → recruits native His-Purkinje system → nearly physiological conduction. LBBAP delivers pacing deep into the LV septum → activates the LV from within. Both can achieve narrow QRS and resynchronisation without the coronary sinus lead (which can be difficult to place). Evidence is growing; not yet standard-of-care but increasingly used in CRT non-responders or failed CRT lead placement.

## Left ventricular assist device (LVAD)

### What it does

An LVAD is a mechanical pump implanted inside or alongside the heart that directly pumps blood from the LV apex to the ascending aorta — bypassing the failing LV myocardium. Modern LVADs (HeartMate 3, HeartWare HVAD) are continuous-flow centrifugal or axial pumps that provide 4–10 L/min of cardiac output continuously.

### Indications

- Bridge to transplant (BTT): keeps a transplant-listed patient alive until a donor organ is available (can take months to years)
- Destination therapy (DT): for patients who are not transplant candidates due to age, comorbidities, or anatomical reasons. The LVAD is the permanent treatment. REMATCH trial: LVAD vs optimal medical therapy in transplant-ineligible Stage D HF — 52% relative risk reduction in mortality at 1 year.
- Bridge to recovery: in some reversible cardiomyopathies (acute myocarditis, peripartum CMP, tachycardia-mediated CMP), an LVAD provides haemodynamic support while the native heart recovers, then the LVAD is explanted.
- Bridge to decision: when prognosis is uncertain, LVAD buys time for further assessment.

### LVAD complications

- Stroke: thromboembolic events from pump thrombosis or pump-related flow disturbances. Required anticoagulation (warfarin INR 2–3 + aspirin in most protocols).
- Bleeding: especially GI bleeding — continuous-flow LVADs reduce pulse pressure → acquired von Willebrand factor deficiency (shear forces degrade large vWF multimers) → mucosal bleeding from angiodysplasia.
- Driveline infection: the driveline exits the skin (percutaneous driveline to the external controller) → chronic infection risk. Most common late complication.
- Right heart failure: LVAD unloads the LV → LV decompresses → septal position shifts → RV can be compromised. Post-LVAD RV failure (occurring in ~20%) is a major cause of early LVAD mortality.
- Device malfunction: pump thrombosis → sudden loss of flow → haemodynamic collapse.

Exam tip: The ICD timing rules — commit these to memory: Post-MI: implant ≥40 days after acute MI (DINAMIT, IRIS)
New HFrEF: reassess EF after ≥3 months of optimal GDMT (reverse remodelling may raise EF above threshold)
NYHA IV inpatient: ICD implant generally not indicated (poor short-term prognosis; exception: Bridge to transplant candidate or LVAD bridge)
Secondary prevention: no waiting period — implant as soon as clinically stable after the index arrhythmic event

Checkpoint: A 58-year-old with non-ischaemic DCM (EF 30%) has been on maximum-tolerated GDMT (sacubitril/valsartan 97/103 mg BD, carvedilol 25 mg BD, eplerenone 50 mg OD, dapagliflozin 10 mg OD) for 6 months. Repeat echo: EF still 30%. ECG: LBBB with QRS 164 ms. NYHA Class III. What device therapy is indicated, and what combined device approach is most appropriate?
CRT-D — cardiac resynchronisation therapy combined with an implantable defibrillator. The indications are met: EF ≤35% (EF 30%), LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms (164 ms), NYHA Class III, and ≥3 months of optimal GDMT without EF recovery. All four criteria for CRT Class I indication are met. The CRT will address the LBBB dyssynchrony (which is likely contributing to the persistently low EF — CRT-induced reverse remodelling may improve EF from 30% to 40–50% over the next 6 months). The defibrillator component is added because EF ≤35% + NYHA II–III meets primary prevention ICD criteria. The CRT-D addresses both problems simultaneously. Expected outcomes post-implant: ~70–80% chance of meaningful EF improvement (CRT response) given LBBB ≥150 ms. If EF improves to >35% at 6–12 months post-CRT, the ICD component remains — EF may fluctuate, and the primary prevention indication was met at the time of implant.

sections.body:
ADHF is the most common cardiac cause of hospitalisation worldwide. Managing it well requires understanding the triggers that cause decompensation, the haemodynamic profile at presentation, and the evidence for each acute intervention — particularly which drugs help and which harm.

## What causes decompensation?

Stable HF patients decompensate when a new stress tips the balance from compensated to uncompensated. Identifying and correcting the precipitant is as important as treating the congestion:

Precipitant | Mechanism | Specific management
Non-compliance with medications or fluid/salt restriction | Loss of neurohormonal blockade → RAAS upregulation; Na/water retention | Re-education, address barriers (cost, side effects, complexity). Most common precipitant worldwide.
New-onset AF or uncontrolled AF with rapid rate | Loss of atrial kick + tachycardia → reduced LV filling + reduced coronary perfusion → acute pump failure | Rate control (BB, digoxin) or cardioversion if recent onset and haemodynamically unstable
Ischaemia / acute MI | Loss of additional myocardium → sudden EF drop → acute failure | Urgent coronary assessment; reperfusion if STEMI or high-risk NSTEMI
Hypertensive crisis | Acute ↑↑ afterload → LV cannot eject → acute pulmonary oedema (often with preserved or even high EF — "flash pulmonary oedema") | IV vasodilators (nitrates, nitroprusside) urgently; BP reduction
Infection / sepsis | Cytokine-mediated myocardial depression + volume shifts + tachycardia | Antibiotics, source control, haemodynamic support
Anaemia | Reduced O₂ carrying capacity → high-output demand on failing heart → decompensation | Treat underlying cause; IV iron (Chapter 11); transfusion if severe
New valve lesion | Acute MR (papillary muscle ischaemia), acute AR (endocarditis), worsening AS | Echo urgently; surgical consultation if severe
NSAID use | Na/water retention + direct renal vasoconstriction → volume overload + AKI | Stop NSAID immediately; resume GDMT; support renal function

## Clinical presentation of ADHF — the Killip-Stevenson matrix

ADHF presentations are classified by haemodynamic profile (as discussed in Chapter 3 — the Forrester-Stevenson profiles). This determines the immediate treatment approach:

### Profile B — "Warm and wet" (most common, ~70% of ADHF admissions)

Adequate perfusion with significant congestion. The LV output is still maintained (warm peripheries) but fluid overload produces dyspnoea, oedema, and raised JVP. These patients respond reliably to diuretics.

### Profile C — "Cold and wet" (cardiogenic shock — ~8–10% of ADHF)

Both reduced perfusion and congestion. Worst prognosis. Requires inotropes and/or MCS. See ACS Guide Chapter 11 for the full management algorithm.

### Profile L — "Cold and dry" (<5%)

Low perfusion without congestion — often from over-diuresis, biventricular failure with RV failure dominating, or haemoconcentration. Do not give more diuretics. Cautious fluid challenge or reduce diuretic dose.

## Intravenous diuresis — the cornerstone of ADHF treatment

Loop diuretics remain the most effective acute therapy for congestion. Key principles:

- IV furosemide is more reliable than oral in acute HF: Gut oedema in acute HF impairs oral furosemide absorption. IV administration bypasses this. Switch to oral when oral bioavailability is adequate (usually when patient is decongested and eating).
- Starting dose: Use the equivalent of the patient's daily oral furosemide dose as IV bolus. First-time HF patient: furosemide 40 mg IV bolus. Patient already on furosemide 80 mg OD chronically: give 80 mg IV bolus (or higher if resistant).
- Monitoring response: Target urine output 100–200 mL/hr in the first few hours. A response <100 mL/hr at 2 hours → double the dose or add a second diuretic class.
- DOSE trial (2011): high-dose diuresis (2.5× daily oral dose) vs low-dose — equivalent clinical outcomes but high-dose produced more diuresis with acceptable transient worsening of creatinine. Current practice: use adequate (not timid) dosing; transient creatinine rise is expected and acceptable if the patient is decongesting.
- Diuretic resistance: When loop diuretics lose efficacy, possible causes: insufficient dose; NSAID use; reduced renal perfusion; hypoalbuminaemia (albumin binds furosemide — free drug fraction reduced). Solutions: increase dose, add thiazide-type diuretic (metolazone 2.5–5 mg OD — creates "sequential nephron blockade"), continuous IV furosemide infusion (more consistent diuresis than intermittent boluses in resistant HF), ultrafiltration in refractory cases.

Key concept: Worsening creatinine during IV diuresis ≠ harm — "cardiorenal haematoconcentration" is a sign of effective decongestion
It seems counterintuitive: as you diurese a congested patient, the creatinine often rises. The reflex is to stop the diuretics to "protect the kidneys." This is usually wrong. In most cases, the creatinine rise is from haemoconcentration (losing water from a congested patient) — the absolute GFR may not have changed significantly. The landmark data (DOSE trial, Mullens analysis) showed that worsening creatinine during decongestion does not predict worse in-hospital or 60-day outcomes when the patient is successfully decongested. The right question is not "is the creatinine rising?" but "is the patient decongesting?" As long as diuresis is occurring and creatinine rise is <30% from baseline and not accelerating, continue diuresis. The cardiorenal syndrome (genuine GFR fall from diuresis) is differentiated by persistent high BNP/filling pressures alongside creatinine rise — the congestion is driving the renal impairment, not the diuretic.

## Vasodilators in acute HF

### IV nitrates

IV glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) or isosorbide dinitrate reduces preload (venous dilation) and, at higher doses, afterload (arterial dilation). Particularly useful in "flash pulmonary oedema" from hypertensive emergency (acute high afterload state — reduce SVR rapidly). Also useful in symptomatic relief of acute dyspnoea. Contraindicated in hypotension (SBP <90), RV infarction (preload-dependent), and recent PDE5 inhibitor use.

### Sodium nitroprusside

Potent mixed venous and arterial vasodilator. Most effective in high-SVR states (hypertensive acute HF, acute severe MR). Requires invasive arterial blood pressure monitoring (causes precipitous BP falls). Metabolised to cyanide — avoid prolonged high-dose infusions in renal failure.

### Nesiritide (BNP infusion)

IV recombinant BNP — natriuretic, diuretic, vasodilatory. ASCEND-HF trial: nesiritide reduced dyspnoea modestly but did not reduce mortality or 30-day readmission and increased hypotension. Not routinely recommended.

## Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) in acute pulmonary oedema

NIV (CPAP or BiPAP) rapidly improves oxygenation and reduces work of breathing in acute pulmonary oedema by:

- Applying positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) → keeps alveoli open → improves gas exchange
- Reducing preload (↑ intrathoracic pressure → reduces venous return)
- Reducing afterload (↑ intrathoracic pressure → reduces transmural LV wall stress)

3CPO trial: CPAP and BiPAP both significantly faster than standard oxygen in improving dyspnoea and oxygenation; no mortality difference between CPAP and BiPAP. CPAP 5–10 cmH₂O is first-line NIV in acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. BiPAP (BiLevel) preferred if CO₂ retention. Early NIV reduces need for intubation.

## GDMT during acute hospitalisation — continue, hold, or modify?

One of the most clinically important decisions during ADHF admission:

- Loop diuretics: increase dose for decongestion — mandatory
- Beta-blockers: continue if possible. COMET data and meta-analyses: continuing BB during ADHF (at same or reduced dose) associated with better outcomes than stopping. Stop only in cardiogenic shock, severe bradycardia, or haemodynamic instability requiring inotropes.
- ACEi/ARNi: hold temporarily if SBP <90, creatinine rising significantly (>30%), or K⁺ >5.5. Restart at lowest dose once stable.
- MRA: hold if K⁺ >5.0 or creatinine significantly worsening. Resume once electrolytes normalise.
- SGLT2i: hold during acute illness with significant haemoconcentration (to reduce DKA risk). Restart before discharge when volume status is normalised.

Exam tip: The pre-discharge checklist — the intervention that most reduces 30-day readmission: Patient is clinically euvolaemic (no resting dyspnoea, no significant oedema, JVP normal)
BNP/NT-proBNP is at least 30% lower than admission level (not necessarily normal — but significantly reduced)
All four GDMT drugs prescribed and at the highest tolerated dose
Electrolytes checked within 24h of discharge and normal
Outpatient follow-up booked within 7 days of discharge (30-day readmission rate is highest in the first week)
Patient education completed: daily weights, fluid restriction, salt restriction, when to call for help (weight gain >2 kg in 48h)
Precipitant addressed (AF rate controlled, infection treated, NSAID stopped)

Checkpoint: A 70-year-old known HFrEF patient on furosemide 40 mg OD, bisoprolol 5 mg OD, sacubitril/valsartan 49/51 mg BD, and dapagliflozin 10 mg presents with 2-day history of worsening dyspnoea and +3 bilateral pitting oedema. On admission: BP 100/70, HR 88, SpO₂ 90% on air, bibasal crackles to mid-zones, JVP elevated 10 cm, creatinine 130 µmol/L (baseline 110). What are the first four things you do?
1. Supplemental oxygen via face mask — SpO₂ 90% requires immediate correction. Target SpO₂ ≥94%. Prepare CPAP if SpO₂ does not improve with face mask O₂ (NIV is likely needed given bilateral mid-zone crackles suggesting moderate pulmonary oedema). 2. IV furosemide 80 mg bolus — he is on 40 mg OD oral furosemide as baseline; in acute decompensation, administer his equivalent daily dose IV (or 2× his daily dose per DOSE trial principles). IV is essential due to likely gut oedema impairing oral absorption. Start urine output monitoring — expect >100 mL/hr. If inadequate response at 2 hours, escalate to 120 mg IV. 3. Hold sacubitril/valsartan temporarily — BP 100/70 is low; adding the vasodilatory/afterload-reducing effect of ARNi could drop BP further acutely. Hold today; reassess when volume status improves and BP stabilises. Similarly hold dapagliflozin during the acute phase (risk of dehydration and haemoconcentration from dual diuresis). 4. Identify the precipitant — check ECG (new AF? ischaemic changes?), blood glucose (SGLT2i + acute illness = DKA risk), FBC (anaemia?), troponin (acute MI?), CRP/WBC (infection?), check medication compliance history. Treating the cause is as important as treating the congestion. Continue bisoprolol at reduced dose (down to 2.5 mg OD) — do not stop it entirely. Admit for IV diuresis and monitoring.

HFpEF accounts for half of all heart failure and has no proven mortality-reducing therapy except SGLT2 inhibitors. Understanding why it resists treatment requires understanding why it is physiologically distinct from HFrEF — and why treating it like HFrEF is not just ineffective, but dangerous.

## What HFpEF actually is

HFpEF is defined by HF symptoms, a preserved EF (≥50%), and evidence of elevated filling pressures or diastolic dysfunction — but without another structural explanation. The fundamental problem is not systolic dysfunction (the heart squeezes adequately — EF is normal) but diastolic dysfunction: the LV is stiff and cannot relax properly, impairing filling and raising filling pressures at rest or with exercise.

HFpEF is not a single disease — it is a syndrome of multiple overlapping conditions with different dominant mechanisms:

- Hypertensive heart disease — pressure overload → concentric hypertrophy → stiff, non-compliant LV. The most common cause.
- Obesity — pericardial fat, increased epicardial fat, systemic inflammation, metabolic effects → diastolic dysfunction + elevated filling pressures + limited ability to increase HR with exercise (chronotropic incompetence)
- Diabetes — glycosylation of myocardial proteins, microvascular disease → diabetic cardiomyopathy → diastolic dysfunction
- Infiltrative disease — amyloid (ATTR/AL), sarcoidosis — infiltration of the myocardium makes it stiff (see Chapter 10)
- Ageing — fibrosis, reduced myocardial compliance with age
- AF — both cause and consequence of HFpEF; AF removes the atrial kick that the stiff LV depends on for late diastolic filling → dramatic symptom worsening

Key concept: HFpEF kills by impairing exercise capacity and fluid regulation — not by failing to eject at rest
At rest, a patient with HFpEF may look relatively well. But exercise reveals the problem: the stiff LV cannot increase its filling volume with exercise (the Starling curve is shifted — to increase SV you need higher filling pressures, but the stiff LV requires very high filling pressures to expand). So exercise → HR rises (OK) but SV can barely increase (limited stroke volume reserve) → CO rises inadequately → exercise intolerance, dyspnoea on exertion. Many HFpEF patients have normal BNP and near-normal echo at rest — the diagnosis requires exercise stress echocardiography or invasive haemodynamics to unmask the elevated filling pressures that only appear with exercise.

## Why the HFrEF drugs don't work in HFpEF

This is one of the most intellectually important concepts in HF medicine:

Drug class | Why it works in HFrEF | Why it fails in HFpEF
ACEi/ARB | Reduces Ang II → reduces fibrosis, afterload → EF improves with reverse remodelling over months | PEP-CHF (perindopril): trend toward benefit but trial underpowered. CHARM-Preserved (candesartan): modest reduction in HF hospitalisations but no mortality benefit. The pathology in HFpEF is a stiff LV, not a dilated failing LV — reducing afterload minimally affects filling-pressure-driven disease.
Beta-blockers | Reduces toxic SNS signalling, allows reverse remodelling, reduces HR to improve diastolic filling time | In HFpEF, slower HR actually worsens exercise tolerance — the stiff LV can only increase CO by increasing HR (SV cannot increase much). A beta-blocker that slows HR limits the only compensatory mechanism for exercise. No mortality trial has shown BB benefit in HFpEF.
MRA | Blocks aldosterone → reduces fibrosis → EF improves | TOPCAT trial (spironolactone in HFpEF): reduction in HF hospitalisation in the Americas subgroup but no mortality benefit overall. Post-hoc analysis questioned trial quality. Inconclusive — not a Class I indication.
SGLT2i | Reduces preload, direct cardioprotection | WORKS — EMPEROR-Preserved (empagliflozin) and DELIVER (dapagliflozin) showed significant reduction in HF hospitalisation and worsening HF in HFpEF. These are the only drugs with proven outcome benefit in HFpEF. Mortality reduction trend but not yet statistically significant. Current recommendation: SGLT2i for all HFpEF (EF ≥50%).

## HFpEF treatment — the current evidence base

### What is proven (Class I or IIa in ESC 2021)

- SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin or dapagliflozin): reduce HF hospitalisation. Start in all symptomatic HFpEF patients without contraindication.
- Diuretics (loop ± thiazide): symptom relief from congestion. The mainstay of symptomatic treatment. Use the lowest effective dose — the stiff LV is preload-sensitive, and over-diuresis drops filling pressures and reduces SV → low output symptoms.
- Treat comorbidities aggressively: the most impactful intervention in HFpEF is treating the underlying conditions that caused or worsen it — HTN (target BP <130/80), DM (SGLT2i/GLP-1 preferred), AF (rate or rhythm control), obesity (weight loss significantly improves diastolic function and exercise capacity — STEP-HFpEF trial: semaglutide in obese HFpEF → 39% improvement in 6-min walk distance), anaemia, sleep apnoea (CPAP).

### GLP-1 receptor agonists — the new HFpEF drug?

Semaglutide (GLP-1 RA) in the STEP-HFpEF trial (2023): in obese HFpEF patients, weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg SC reduced symptoms (KCCQ score), 6-min walk distance, CRP, and body weight significantly vs placebo. This is a major development — HFpEF driven by obesity may respond to aggressive weight reduction via GLP-1 agonism. Not yet a guideline class I recommendation but rapidly becoming standard practice.

Clinical link: The single most important management principle in HFpEF: do not over-diurese. In HFrEF, aggressive diuresis is a cornerstone of ADHF treatment. In HFpEF, the stiff, thick-walled LV is exquisitely preload-sensitive — it needs high filling pressures to maintain adequate SV. Too little volume → the LV cannot fill adequately → SV drops → low output symptoms (fatigue, dizziness, confusion, worsening renal function). Over-diuresis in HFpEF is a common and consequential error. Target: clinical euvolaemia, not absolute dryness. Maintain adequate fluid status while treating congestion symptoms.

Exam tip: Diagnosing HFpEF when BNP is normal — exercise stress echo (ESE): Many patients with HFpEF have normal or borderline BNP at rest, normal resting echo, but typical exertional dyspnoea. The diagnosis requires unmasking elevated filling pressures that only appear with exercise. Exercise stress echocardiography: patient exercises on a supine bicycle ergometer. Echo parameters measured at peak exercise: E/e' >15 at peak exercise (elevated filling pressures on exertion), peak PASP >60 mmHg (secondary pulmonary hypertension), reduced functional reserve. Invasive haemodynamics (Swan-Ganz during exercise) is the gold standard. HFpEF is a disease of exercise haemodynamics, not resting haemodynamics.

Checkpoint: A 72-year-old obese woman (BMI 38) with HTN, AF, and T2DM presents with exertional dyspnoea on minimal activity. Echo: EF 58%, E/A 0.9, e' 6 cm/s bilateral, E/e' 13, LAVI 40 mL/m², moderate concentric LVH, PASP 45 mmHg, TAPSE 18 mm. BNP 95 pg/mL. What is the diagnosis, and list four management interventions ranked by evidence level?
HFpEF — the criteria are met: HF symptoms (exertional dyspnoea), preserved EF (58%), and evidence of elevated filling pressures (E/e' 13 — borderline but combined with LAVI 40 mL/m², PASP 45 mmHg, and LVH makes HFpEF the diagnosis). BNP 95 pg/mL is mildly elevated above the non-acute rule-out threshold of 35 pg/mL, and is lower than in HFrEF partly because of her obesity. Management by evidence level: (1) SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin or dapagliflozin 10 mg OD) — Class I/IIa, only drug class with proven outcome benefit in HFpEF, also benefits her DM; (2) AF management — she has AF without atrial kick on a preload-dependent stiff LV. Rate control (BB or digoxin) or rhythm control (consider cardioversion and antiarrhythmic) — rhythm control is increasingly preferred in HFpEF+AF (AFFIRM subgroup, EAST-AFNET 4); (3) Blood pressure control to <130/80 mmHg — treating the hypertensive cause of her LVH directly addresses the HFpEF mechanism; (4) Weight reduction — GLP-1 RA (semaglutide) or intensive lifestyle intervention; obesity is a major driver of her HFpEF (STEP-HFpEF data). Diuretics for symptom relief — use cautiously given HFpEF preload sensitivity.

sections.body:
Every arrhythmia is a deviation from normal electrical behaviour. Understanding what normal looks like — the action potential, the conduction system, the ionic currents — is the only way to understand why arrhythmias occur and why specific drugs work on specific channels.

## The cardiac action potential

A cardiac action potential is the sequence of electrical events in a single myocyte. Different cell types have different action potential shapes, reflecting different ionic channel compositions:

### Ventricular myocyte — the "fast-response" action potential

Five phases:

- Phase 0 — Rapid depolarisation: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open rapidly (Na⁺ rushes in → fast depolarisation from −85 mV to +20 mV). This creates the fast upstroke. Drugs that block Na⁺ channels (class Ia, Ib, Ic) slow this phase → widen the QRS.
- Phase 1 — Early repolarisation: Na⁺ channels rapidly inactivate; transient outward K⁺ current (Ito) begins repolarisation. Notch on the action potential upstroke. Prominent in ventricular epicardium — reduced in endocardium. The epicardial-endocardial Ito difference is the cellular basis of the J-wave syndromes (Brugada, early repolarisation).
- Phase 2 — Plateau: L-type Ca²⁺ channels open (Ca²⁺ in) balanced by K⁺ out (IKr, IKs). The long plateau is unique to cardiac muscle — it prevents tetanic contractions (unlike skeletal muscle). This phase corresponds to the ST segment on the ECG. L-type Ca²⁺ channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil, DHP-CCBs) affect this phase. The plateau creates the refractory period — the heart cannot be re-stimulated during this phase.
- Phase 3 — Rapid repolarisation: K⁺ channels (IKr and IKs — the rapid and slow delayed rectifier K⁺ currents) dominate → rapid repolarisation back to resting potential. Drugs blocking IKr (most class III antiarrhythmics — amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide) prolong this phase → prolong the QT interval → risk of Torsades de Pointes.
- Phase 4 — Resting membrane potential: −85 mV, maintained by inward rectifier K⁺ current (IK1). The cell is at rest, awaiting the next stimulus from the conducting system.

### SA node / AV node — the "slow-response" action potential

SA and AV nodal cells do not have fast Na⁺ channels. Their depolarisation relies entirely on L-type Ca²⁺ channels → slower, smaller upstroke (unlike the sharp phase 0 of ventricular cells).

Phase 4 — Spontaneous depolarisation (pacemaker potential): the "funny current" (If, carried by HCN channels) and other currents cause the resting membrane potential to slowly drift upward from −65 mV toward the threshold. When threshold is reached → Ca²⁺-driven depolarisation. This spontaneous phase 4 depolarisation is what makes SA and AV nodes automatic. It is the molecular basis of the heartbeat.

Ivabradine blocks If → slows the rate of phase 4 depolarisation → slows HR. Beta-blockers reduce the rate of phase 4 depolarisation (via reduced cAMP). Non-DHP CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem) block L-type Ca²⁺ channels in nodal tissue → slow AV nodal conduction.

Key concept: The AV node is slow-channel tissue — that is why blocking L-type Ca²⁺ channels (verapamil, diltiazem) slows AV conduction and terminates nodal re-entry tachycardias
The AV node has no fast Na⁺ channels. Its conduction depends entirely on slow Ca²⁺-driven depolarisation. This is what makes the AV node: (1) slow — accounts for the PR interval delay; (2) decremental — conduction slows progressively with rapid stimulation (Wenckebach phenomenon); (3) sensitive to Ca²⁺ channel blockers and adenosine. When you give adenosine or verapamil, you are pharmacologically blocking the Ca²⁺-dependent depolarisation of the AV node — slowing or blocking AV conduction completely. This terminates any re-entrant tachycardia that uses the AV node as part of its circuit (AVNRT, AVRT). It does NOT terminate atrial tachycardia or flutter — it temporarily slows the ventricular rate (by blocking AV conduction) and may reveal the underlying atrial rhythm, but the tachycardia continues in the atrium.

## The cardiac conduction system

The normal pathway of electrical activation:

1. SA node (right atrium, superior aspect of the crista terminalis, near SVC-RA junction) — generates the sinus impulse at 60–100 bpm. Automaticity is highest here — it suppresses all lower pacemakers (overdrive suppression).
2. Internodal pathways — three preferential conduction pathways conduct the impulse through the right atrium toward the AV node. Simultaneous left atrial activation via Bachmann's bundle (interatrial conduction).
3. AV node (triangle of Koch — bounded by the coronary sinus ostium, tendon of Todaro, and tricuspid annulus) — the physiological "gatekeeper." Introduces a delay (PR interval ~120–200 ms) that allows atrial emptying before ventricular contraction. Only normal pathway for conduction from atria to ventricles (in the absence of an accessory pathway).
4. Bundle of His — exits the AV node, runs through the membranous interventricular septum. Bundle of His conduction is rapid and non-decremental.
5. Left and right bundle branches — split at the upper interventricular septum. RBB — thin, long, follows the moderator band to the RV free wall. LBB — thick, fans out into left anterior fascicle (LAF) and left posterior fascicle (LPF).
6. Purkinje fibres — terminal branches of the bundle branches, spread activation through the ventricular endocardium. Rapid conduction → near-simultaneous ventricular activation → narrow QRS (<120 ms).

Diagram: Cardiac conduction system — anatomy and intrinsic rates of escape pacemakers at each level (drawing not carried over)

## Ionic currents and drug targets — the master table

Current | Channel / Carrier | Phase | What blocking it does | Drug examples
INa (fast) | Voltage-gated Na⁺ (Nav1.5) | 0 | Slows phase 0 upstroke → slower conduction velocity → wider QRS; raises activation threshold → reduces automaticity | Class Ia (quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide); Class Ib (lidocaine, mexiletine); Class Ic (flecainide, propafenone)
If (funny current) | HCN4 channels | 4 | Slows phase 4 diastolic depolarisation → reduces automaticity → slower HR | Ivabradine (selective If blocker)
ICa,L (L-type) | Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ (Cav1.2) | 0 (nodal), 2 | In nodal cells: slows depolarisation → slows SA rate + AV conduction. In ventricular cells: shortens plateau (phase 2). | Diltiazem, verapamil (non-DHP — nodal effects); DHP-CCBs (nifedipine — peripheral vasodilation, minimal nodal effect)
IKr (rapid delayed rectifier) | hERG channel (KCNH2) | 3 | Blocks repolarisation → prolongs action potential duration → prolongs QT interval → TdP risk | Class III (amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide, ibutilide); many non-cardiac drugs (antibiotics, antipsychotics)
IKs (slow delayed rectifier) | KCNQ1 + KCNE1 | 3 | Loss-of-function mutations: LQTS type 1 (LQT1) — the most common congenital LQTS subtype | No drugs target this; mutations cause LQTS
β-adrenergic receptor | β1 (Gs → ↑ cAMP) | 4 + 0 | Blocking β1: ↓ phase 4 depolarisation rate (↓ automaticity), ↓ ICa,L → slower SA + AV conduction, ↑ VF threshold | Metoprolol, bisoprolol, carvedilol (Class II)

Exam tip: The hERG channel is the Achilles heel of drug safety in cardiology. The hERG (human ether-à-go-go related gene) potassium channel carries IKr — the dominant repolarising current in phase 3. It has a large, hydrophobic binding pocket that promiscuously binds many lipophilic drugs. Drug-induced hERG block is the most common cause of acquired QT prolongation and Torsades de Pointes. Classes affected: certain antibiotics (azithromycin, fluoroquinolones), antipsychotics (haloperidol, droperidol), antidepressants (TCAs), antiemetics (metoclopramide, ondansetron at high doses), antifungals (fluconazole), antimalarials (hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine — clinically important in Indonesia). Always check QTc before prescribing these agents, especially in combination with each other or with class III antiarrhythmics.

Checkpoint: A patient receives lidocaine IV for VT. A colleague asks: "Why is lidocaine safe for VT suppression but dangerous if given for SVT?" Explain using the action potential and channel-specific binding.
Lidocaine is a class Ib Na⁺ channel blocker with use-dependent, voltage-dependent channel block — it preferentially binds the Na⁺ channel when it is in the open or inactivated state (which occurs at fast rates and in depolarised tissue). Its properties: fast on-rate at high frequency, fast off-rate at normal frequency. This means: in fast-firing ventricular tissue during VT (very rapid, partially depolarised from ischaemia) → lidocaine blocks the Na⁺ channel effectively → slows conduction → terminates re-entry. But in normal-rate sinus rhythm or in SVT: the Na⁺ channel spends most time in the rested state (lidocaine dissociates quickly between beats) → minimal effect. Why dangerous in SVT? SVT is most commonly AVNRT or AVRT — these involve the AV node (which has no fast Na⁺ channels). Lidocaine has essentially no AV nodal effect. If you give lidocaine thinking the wide complex is SVT with aberrancy, and it is actually VT — lidocaine may work (correctly). But if it is truly SVT with rate response that causes haemodynamic compromise — lidocaine does nothing and you have wasted time. The real danger is administering verapamil for presumed SVT in a patient with actual VT (ventricular tachycardia misidentified as SVT with aberrancy) — verapamil causes vasodilation and negative inotropy → haemodynamic collapse in VT. This distinction is covered in detail in Chapter 8.

WPW is the arrhythmia where the correct drug for one tachycardia is deadly in another. One patient, one accessory pathway — but the specific tachycardia determines whether you give adenosine or avoid it entirely. Getting this wrong is fatal.

## The accessory pathway — anatomy and pre-excitation

An accessory pathway (AP) is an abnormal muscle bundle that forms a direct electrical connection between the atrium and ventricle outside the AV node, usually around the tricuspid or mitral annulus. When conductive in the anterograde direction: the AP conducts the sinus impulse from the atrium directly to the ventricle, bypassing the AV node. Result: the ventricle starts activating earlier than normal (pre-excitation), producing the characteristic delta wave.

Delta wave: a slurring of the initial QRS upstroke, created by the early, slow ventricular activation via the AP (AP conduction is muscle-to-muscle, without fast Purkinje spread → slow, "slurred" initial depolarisation). The delta wave is immediately followed by normal QRS (once the His-Purkinje wave arrives and takes over, producing rapid ventricular activation).

WPW pattern (ECG): delta wave + short PR interval (<120 ms — the AV node delay is bypassed) + wide QRS (total QRS = delta wave pre-excitation + His-Purkinje activation merged). The PR is short because the AP conducts without AV nodal delay.

WPW syndrome = WPW pattern + symptomatic arrhythmias.

## Accessory pathway location and ECG localisation

The delta wave polarity in different leads tells you where the AP is:

- Negative delta wave in V1 (LBBB-like pre-excitation) → left-sided AP (most common — left free wall)
- Positive delta wave in V1 (RBBB-like pre-excitation) → right-sided AP
- Negative delta wave in inferior leads (II, III, aVF) → posteroseptal AP
- Positive delta in all leads → anteroseptal or left lateral AP

## Three tachyarrhythmias in WPW — completely different management

### 1. Orthodromic AVRT (narrow complex)

Anterograde via AV node → retrograde via AP. Narrow QRS (normal His-Purkinje activation), visible P after QRS (retrograde P, negative in inferior leads), regular at 150–250 bpm. Management: vagal manoeuvres → adenosine is SAFE (the AV node is the anterograde limb — blocking it terminates the circuit). Non-DHP CCBs also safe. Ablate the AP to prevent recurrence.

### 2. Antidromic AVRT (wide complex)

Anterograde via AP → retrograde via AV node. Wide, fully pre-excited QRS (bizarre wide complex, maximum delta waves, no normal narrow QRS component), P waves after QRS. Rate 150–250 bpm, regular. Management: IV procainamide (blocks AP conduction) or cardioversion. Adenosine is relatively contraindicated — blocks the AV node, which is the retrograde limb. It may terminate the tachycardia (if the circuit breaks by blocking the retrograde AV nodal limb) but can accelerate conduction down the AP and potentially precipitate AF with rapid AP conduction. Safer to use procainamide or cardiovert.

### 3. AF with WPW — the most dangerous scenario

AF can conduct down the AP directly (rather than through the AV node). If the AP has a short refractory period, AF wavefronts conduct rapidly down the AP → extremely rapid ventricular rates (200–300+ bpm) with wide, irregular, bizarre QRS complexes. This can degenerate to VF.

Warning: AF + WPW is a medical emergency. AV nodal blockers (adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin) are absolutely contraindicated. Blocking the AV node in AF+WPW forces ALL AF wavefronts through the AP → ventricular rate 250–300+ bpm → ventricular fibrillation → death. The drug that saves every other SVT patient kills a WPW patient with AF. Correct treatment for haemodynamically unstable AF+WPW: immediate DC cardioversion. For haemodynamically stable: IV procainamide (slows AP conduction) or IV flecainide (blocks AP). Never adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers, or digoxin in pre-excited AF.

## ECG recognition of AF + WPW

The pattern is unmistakable when you know what to look for: very rapid, irregular, wide complex tachycardia with continuously changing QRS morphology (as beats come from different combinations of AP conduction and AV nodal conduction → varying degrees of pre-excitation). Some beats are narrow (conducted via AV node — sinus cycle captured), some are wide delta waves (conducted via AP), some are intermediate (fusion). This creates the irregular, morphologically variable wide complex tachycardia that is the hallmark of AF+WPW.

## Risk stratification and long-term management

Not all AP-possessing patients are equal. The key risk factor for SCD in WPW is a short AP refractory period (<250 ms) — this determines how fast the ventricle can be driven during AF. Assessment: EP study with AP refractory period measurement, or electrophysiology-guided risk stratification.

High-risk features: AP refractory period <250 ms, history of rapid pre-excited AF, aborted SCA, inducible ventricular arrhythmia at EP study. These patients require AP ablation regardless of symptoms.

Asymptomatic WPW: ESC 2019 guidelines recommend non-invasive and/or invasive risk stratification. If low risk → observe. If high risk or preferred by patient → AP ablation. Ablation offers cure: success rate 95%+ for left free-wall APs; slightly less for septal APs; risk of AV block only for parahisian APs.

Checkpoint: A 26-year-old athlete has WPW pattern on routine ECG (short PR, delta waves, wide QRS). He has never had palpitations. His parents want to know his risk. An exercise test shows that the delta wave disappears abruptly at a heart rate of 160 bpm during exercise. What does this finding tell you about his AP, and what does it mean for his risk of SCD?
Abrupt disappearance of the delta wave during exercise at a specific HR is a reassuring finding called "intermittent pre-excitation" or "exercise-induced loss of pre-excitation." When the sinus rate reaches 160 bpm, the AP can no longer keep up (the AP's refractory period is longer than the RR interval at 160 bpm = AP refractory period ~375 ms at HR 160). When the AP becomes refractory at faster rates, the ventricle is activated entirely via the normal AV node → delta wave disappears → QRS narrows. This implies the AP has a relatively long refractory period (≥375 ms), which means: if this patient developed AF, the AP would not be able to conduct AF wavefronts faster than ~160 bpm → ventricular rate during AF+WPW would not be dangerously fast → lower risk of VF. ESC guidelines interpretation: non-invasive risk stratification (exercise test with abrupt loss of pre-excitation) suggests low-risk AP. Recommend: EP study to formally measure AP refractory period (confirmatory), consider ablation for definitive cure especially as an athlete. The ACC/AHA guidelines would also support ablation in this setting for peace of mind and to remove any competitive sport restriction.
