sections.body:
AVNRT accounts for 60% of all SVT, AVRT for 30%, focal AT for 10%. Each has a different re-entrant circuit, different P wave position, and different response to ablation. Knowing the circuit predicts the ECG and guides the treatment.

## AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT)

### The circuit

The AV node has two functionally distinct conduction pathways in most people: the slow pathway (posteroinferior approach — slow conduction, short refractory period) and the fast pathway (anterosuperior approach — fast conduction, long refractory period). Normally, an impulse from the atrium uses both pathways, but the fast pathway's impulse arrives at the His bundle first (shorter conduction time despite starting simultaneously).

During typical AVNRT (slow-fast AVNRT, ~90% of cases): a premature atrial contraction arrives when the fast pathway is still refractory → blocks in the fast pathway → conducts slowly down the slow pathway → the His bundle has now recovered → the impulse travels retrogradely back up through the recovered fast pathway to the atrium → re-enters the slow pathway → creates a circuit. The atrium and ventricle are activated nearly simultaneously (slow pathway conducts to the ventricle AND the fast pathway conducts retrogradely to the atrium at the same time).

### ECG signature of typical AVNRT

- Rate 150–250 bpm (usually 160–200 bpm)
- Regular, narrow QRS (normal QRS duration unless aberrant conduction)
- P waves hidden within or immediately after the QRS (nearly simultaneous atrial and ventricular activation) — "pseudo-R'" in V1 (retrograde P buried in end of QRS creates a small terminal deflection) or "pseudo-S" in inferior leads
- RP interval < PR interval (RP < 70 ms — very short, because the retrograde P almost coincides with the QRS)

## AV re-entrant tachycardia (AVRT)

### The circuit

AVRT uses an accessory pathway (an abnormal muscle bundle connecting the atrium directly to the ventricle — bypassing the AV node) as one limb of the re-entrant circuit and the AV node as the other limb.

- Orthodromic AVRT (~95% of AVRT): impulse travels anterograde through the AV node → ventricle → retrograde through the accessory pathway → atrium → AV node again. Narrow QRS (normal AV node → His → Purkinje activation) unless aberrancy. P wave visible after the QRS (retrograde, negative in inferior leads, RP 70–140 ms — short RP, but longer than in AVNRT).
- Antidromic AVRT (~5% of AVRT): anterograde through the accessory pathway → ventricle (bypassing the AV node) → retrograde through the AV node. Wide QRS (ventricle activated via the accessory pathway, not His-Purkinje → fully pre-excited QRS, delta waves). Looks like VT. Haemodynamically more significant.

Key concept: In AVNRT, the P wave is buried in the QRS or immediately after. In AVRT, the P wave is visible after the QRS. This single distinction identifies the circuit.
The position of the P wave relative to the QRS during SVT reveals how fast the retrograde atrial activation is relative to ventricular activation. In AVNRT: anterograde (slow pathway) and retrograde (fast pathway) activation are nearly simultaneous → P is within or just after the QRS (RP < 70 ms). In AVRT: the retrograde impulse must travel from the ventricle, through the accessory pathway (which may be anywhere around the AV ring), back to the atrium — this takes longer → P is visible after the QRS (RP 70–140 ms). Short RP tachycardias (RP < PR): AVNRT, AVRT, junctional tachycardia. Long RP tachycardias (RP > PR): atypical AVNRT, PJRT (permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia), focal AT, sinus tachycardia.

## Focal atrial tachycardia (AT)

An ectopic focus within the atrium (not involving the AV node) fires rapidly, producing an organised atrial tachycardia at 150–250 bpm. The AV node is a bystander — it just conducts whatever comes from the atrium (at its natural AV nodal conduction limit).

- P wave morphology is different from sinus P (depends on where the focus is — right atrial, left atrial, crista terminalis, pulmonary veins)
- P wave precedes QRS (P before QRS, but RP > PR — long RP tachycardia). The PR interval depends on the AT rate and AV nodal function.
- Vagal manoeuvres and adenosine: slow ventricular rate (temporary AV block) but reveal continuous atrial tachycardia — the AT does not terminate
- Mechanism: enhanced automaticity or triggered activity (DADs) at the focus; focal or micro-re-entry

## Acute management of SVT — the step algorithm

Step 1 — Haemodynamically unstable? → Synchronised cardioversion immediately (100–200 J biphasic)

Step 2 — Vagal manoeuvres: Valsalva (effective in ~50%), carotid sinus massage (contraindicated if carotid bruit / recent stroke / elderly with suspected carotid disease). Modified Valsalva (REVERT trial): Valsalva lying down, then passive leg raise → 43% conversion rate (vs 17% standard).

Step 3 — IV adenosine: 6 mg rapid IV bolus in a large antecubital vein or central line; if no effect after 2 minutes, 12 mg; repeat 12 mg once. Adenosine: rapidly activates IKAdo → hyperpolarises the AV node → transient complete AV block (usually 10–20 seconds) → terminates AVNRT and AVRT. Effect on AT/flutter: AV block temporarily → reveals atrial flutter waves or continuous AT P waves; does not terminate. Patient warning: brief but intense chest tightness, flushing, dyspnoea — must warn the patient.

Step 4 — IV AV nodal blockers: IV verapamil 5–10 mg over 3 min, or IV diltiazem, or IV metoprolol — terminate or slow rate.

Step 5 — Synchronised cardioversion if medical therapy fails and patient symptomatic.

Warning: Adenosine and verapamil are dangerous in pre-excited (WPW) tachycardias. If a patient has a pre-excited wide complex tachycardia (antidromic AVRT, or AF with WPW), blocking the AV node (with adenosine or verapamil) forces ALL conduction through the accessory pathway. If the accessory pathway has a short refractory period, rapid conduction to the ventricle can trigger VF and death. Adenosine is safe in narrow-complex AVRT (orthodromic) because the QRS is narrow, confirming conduction via the normal AV node. Adenosine is dangerous in any wide-complex tachycardia with a delta-wave morphology (pre-excited QRS) — this may be WPW. Chapter 10 covers this fully.

## Long-term management — catheter ablation is curative

- AVNRT ablation: slow pathway modification (radiofrequency ablation of the slow pathway, which is posteroinferior to the AV node). Success rate >98%. Recurrence <3%. Risk of complete AV block (requiring pacemaker) <1%.
- AVRT ablation: ablation of the accessory pathway. Success rate >95%. Risk depends on pathway location — parahisian pathways have ~3–5% AV block risk; others lower.
- Focal AT ablation: map and ablate the focus. Success rate ~85–90% for right atrial foci; slightly lower for left atrial foci.
- Medical alternatives: beta-blockers or non-DHP CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem) for rate control/prevention. Flecainide or propafenone (class Ic) for rhythm control in structurally normal hearts (pill-in-the-pocket strategy for infrequent SVT).

Checkpoint: A 28-year-old woman presents with her third episode of SVT. ECG: regular narrow complex tachycardia 190 bpm, P waves visible as pseudo-R' deflection in V1 and pseudo-S waves in leads II, III, aVF. Modified Valsalva (supine + leg raise) successfully terminates the tachycardia. She asks about cure. What is the diagnosis, what does the P wave position confirm, and what is the curative option and its success rate?
Typical AVNRT (slow-fast). P wave position confirms this: the pseudo-R' in V1 and pseudo-S waves in inferior leads are the hallmark of retrograde P waves buried at the very end of the QRS (RP < 70 ms) — atria and ventricles activated nearly simultaneously, consistent with the slow-fast AVNRT circuit (anterograde via slow pathway to ventricle, retrograde via fast pathway to atrium — both happening at the same time). The modified Valsalva manoeuvre (REVERT trial technique) was used correctly and terminated it — confirming nodal involvement. Curative option: electrophysiology study and slow pathway ablation. Success rate >98%, recurrence <3%, risk of requiring permanent pacemaker <1%. This should be offered as the preferred long-term management over lifelong antiarrhythmic drugs. Alternative if she declines ablation: oral flecainide 100–150 mg as "pill in the pocket" (taken only at onset of SVT, for patients with infrequent but prolonged episodes) — confirm structurally normal heart first (echo), confirm no coronary disease (given her age, low risk).

title: SVT — AVNRT, AVRT, and atrial tachycardia

sections.body:
AF is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and the leading preventable cause of embolic stroke. Its management involves three simultaneous decisions — anticoagulation (the most important), rate control, and rhythm control — each driven by a specific evidence base.

## Classification and epidemiology

Classification | Definition | Clinical implication
Paroxysmal AF | Episodes that terminate spontaneously or with intervention within 7 days | Stroke risk equivalent to persistent AF — anticoagulate regardless of "how short" the episodes are
Persistent AF | Continuous AF lasting >7 days (or requiring cardioversion to terminate) | More likely to require antiarrhythmic drugs or ablation for rhythm control
Long-standing persistent AF | Continuous AF for ≥1 year | Atrial remodelling makes sinus rhythm restoration increasingly difficult
Permanent AF | Decision by patient and clinician to accept AF and no longer attempt rhythm control | Rate control + anticoagulation; rhythm control interventions abandoned

Prevalence: ~3–4% of adults >60 years; 10% of adults >80 years. The "AF epidemic" — aging population, increasing hypertension, obesity, and HF prevalence. In Indonesia: significant burden underdiagnosed, particularly in HTN and rheumatic heart disease populations.

## Mechanism of AF

AF is maintained by: (1) multiple re-entrant wavelets — disorganised electrical wavefronts simultaneously propagating through atrial tissue in multiple directions; (2) focal triggers — ectopic foci, predominantly from the pulmonary vein ostia (PV muscles extend into the PV sleeves, possess automaticity and triggered activity). PV isolation is the basis of catheter ablation. (3) Atrial remodelling substrate — atrial fibrosis (from HTN, HF, age), atrial dilation (from valvular disease), autonomic nervous system changes.

"AF begets AF" — the electrical and structural remodelling from sustained AF makes the atrium more susceptible to further AF, making early rhythm control increasingly important.

## Stroke risk — CHA₂DS₂-VASc score

AF increases stroke risk 5-fold. The annual stroke risk is estimated using CHA₂DS₂-VASc:

Factor | Score | Annual stroke risk at this score
C — Congestive HF (or LVEF <40%) | 1 | 
H — Hypertension | 1
A₂ — Age ≥75 years | 2
D — Diabetes mellitus | 1
S₂ — Stroke / TIA / thromboembolism (prior) | 2
V — Vascular disease (prior MI, PAD, aortic plaque) | 1
A — Age 65–74 years | 1
Sc — Sex category (female) | 1
Maximum score | 9

Anticoagulation decision (ESC 2020 AF guidelines):

- Men: score ≥1 → consider anticoagulation; score ≥2 → anticoagulate
- Women: score ≥2 → consider; score ≥3 → anticoagulate (sex category alone is not sufficient to trigger anticoagulation)
- Score 0 (male) or 1 (female due to sex only) → no anticoagulation needed; reassess annually

Key concept: DOACs are the anticoagulant of choice for AF — they reduce stroke and ICH compared to warfarin with equivalent or better efficacy
Four major DOAC trials in AF: ARISTOTLE (apixaban vs warfarin), ROCKET-AF (rivaroxaban vs warfarin), RELY (dabigatran vs warfarin), ENGAGE-TIMI 48 (edoxaban vs warfarin). All showed DOACs non-inferior or superior to warfarin for stroke prevention, with significantly less intracranial haemorrhage (~50% less ICH than warfarin). DOACs are now preferred over warfarin in all AF patients with non-valvular AF. Exception: warfarin (not DOAC) remains preferred for AF with mechanical heart valves (DOACs failed in RE-ALIGN trial for mechanical valves — higher thrombotic events) and moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis (left atrial blood stasis from MS creates embolic risk not addressed by DOACs in trial data). All other structural heart disease (including HF, biological valves, mild MR) can use DOACs.

## Bleeding risk — HAS-BLED score

HAS-BLED estimates annual bleeding risk: Hypertension (uncontrolled SBP >160), Abnormal renal/liver function, Stroke history, Bleeding history, Labile INR (if on warfarin), Elderly (>65 years), Drugs (antiplatelets, NSAIDs) or alcohol. Score ≥3 = high bleeding risk. However: high bleeding risk is NOT a reason to withhold anticoagulation if stroke risk is significant — it is a reason to correct reversible bleeding risk factors (control BP, stop NSAIDs, monitor INR more closely). The absolute stroke risk reduction from anticoagulation almost always outweighs the absolute bleeding risk increase in high CHA₂DS₂-VASc patients.

## Rate control

Rate control reduces symptoms from tachycardia without attempting to restore sinus rhythm. Target: resting HR <110 bpm (lenient rate control — RACE II trial showed lenient ≤110 bpm non-inferior to strict <80 bpm for outcomes in most patients). Strict <80 bpm for symptomatic patients or those with tachycardia-mediated CMP.

Drug | Mechanism | Use in HFrEF? | Notes
Beta-blockers | β1 blockade → ↓ AV nodal conduction velocity | Yes — preferred (mortality benefit) | Bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol. First-line in most patients.
Non-DHP CCBs (Diltiazem, Verapamil) | Ca²⁺ channel block in AV node → slows conduction | NO — contraindicated in HFrEF (negative inotropy) | Effective rate control. Use in HFpEF or structurally normal heart.
Digoxin | Vagal enhancement → ↓ AV nodal conduction; weak positive inotrope | Yes — use in HFrEF if BB insufficient | Effective at rest; poor rate control with exercise. Narrow therapeutic index. Not first-line alone.
Amiodarone | Multiple channel block including AV nodal | Yes — careful monitoring | Reserve for refractory rate control. Extensive side effects.
AV node ablation + pacemaker | Surgical AV nodal ablation → complete AV block → pacemaker provides ventricular rate | Yes — HIS bundle pacing or CRT pacing preferred | "Ablate and pace" strategy for refractory rate control or if drugs poorly tolerated.

## Rhythm control — rate control vs rhythm control

For decades, the AFFIRM trial (2002) showed rate control ≡ rhythm control for mortality in older patients with AF — and rhythm control added side effects. But AFFIRM enrolled older patients. The landscape has changed:

EAST-AFNET 4 trial (2020): early rhythm control (within 1 year of AF diagnosis) vs usual care — significant reduction in cardiovascular outcomes (CV death, stroke, HF, MI) in patients with recent AF and cardiovascular risk factors. Rhythm control benefit was driven largely by catheter ablation and early antiarrhythmic drug use.

Current paradigm: early rhythm control is preferred in most AF patients, especially those with symptoms and/or cardiovascular risk — but rate control remains an acceptable strategy in selected asymptomatic patients with permanent AF.

### Cardioversion

- Immediate DC cardioversion: for haemodynamically unstable AF (hypotension, pulmonary oedema, acute coronary syndrome from rapid AF) — synchronised shock 120–200 J biphasic
- Elective cardioversion: for persistent AF requiring rhythm control. Requirements: (1) anticoagulate for ≥3 weeks before (to prevent dislodging a pre-formed LA appendage thrombus), then continue ≥4 weeks after (stunning → thrombus forms during recovery of LA function); OR (2) TOE-guided cardioversion (TOE to exclude LAA thrombus → cardiovert → anticoagulate afterwards)
- Pharmacological cardioversion: flecainide 200–300 mg PO (pill-in-the-pocket in structurally normal heart), IV ibutilide, IV vernakalant. Only in structurally normal hearts (no ischaemic CMP, no significant LVH, no HF).

## Catheter ablation for AF

Pulmonary vein isolation (PVI): circumferential radiofrequency or cryoablation around the PV ostia creates electrical isolation of the PVs from the LA → eliminates the most common AF triggers. The cornerstone of AF ablation.

- Paroxysmal AF: success ~70–80% (single procedure, 1-year follow-up); multiple procedures improve to 85%+
- Persistent/long-standing persistent AF: lower success rates (30–60% single procedure), higher recurrence, often requires additional substrate modification (posterior wall isolation, ablation of low-voltage areas)
- CASTLE-AF (HFrEF+AF): AF ablation vs rate control — mortality reduction 38%, HF hospitalisation reduction 44%, EF improvement. Supports ablation in HFrEF+AF.
- Complications: LA oesophageal fistula (rare, <0.1%, fatal), stroke (1–2%), PV stenosis (1–3%), cardiac tamponade (1%), phrenic nerve palsy (temporary, especially with cryo), vascular access complications

Exam tip: Cardioversion in AF duration <48 hours — two approaches and what to choose: AF duration <48 hours AND haemodynamically stable: may cardiovert without prolonged anticoagulation (thrombus is unlikely to have formed in <48 hours) — but still give heparin before cardioversion and anticoagulate for ≥4 weeks after (LA stunning risk regardless of duration). This is the "immediate" approach — standard for recent-onset AF.
AF duration unknown or >48 hours: MUST anticoagulate for ≥3 weeks before elective cardioversion OR perform TOE to exclude LAA thrombus before cardioversion. Proceeding without this invites embolic stroke.
The dangerous scenario: patient presents with "1-day history of AF" but is an unreliable historian with uncontrolled AF (perhaps in permanent AF for months) — always err toward longer anticoagulation or TOE if any doubt about duration.

Checkpoint: A 72-year-old man, BP 148/92, with type 2 DM, no prior stroke, no cardiac disease beyond hypertension. He has paroxysmal AF. His CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is calculated. His GP prescribed aspirin because "AF is a clotting problem and aspirin prevents clots." What is his score, what should he be on, and why is aspirin alone clearly insufficient for AF stroke prevention?
CHA₂DS₂-VASc score: H (hypertension) = 1, A (age 72, in the 65–74 bracket) = 1, D (DM) = 1, V (vascular disease? — not mentioned = 0) = total score = 3. At score ≥2 in a male patient → anticoagulation is indicated. He should be on a DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, or edoxaban) — not aspirin. Why aspirin is insufficient: AF-related stroke is predominantly thromboembolic — clot forms in the left atrial appendage (LAA) where stagnant blood pools due to lack of atrial contraction. This clot is fibrin-rich (requires anticoagulation to prevent and treat). Aspirin inhibits platelet aggregation (platelet-rich clot) — it has essentially no effect on fibrin clots. ACTIVE-A trial confirmed aspirin + clopidogrel is inferior to warfarin for AF stroke prevention. Aspirin alone: only ~22% relative stroke risk reduction in AF (vs warfarin's 64%, DOAC's ≥60%). Aspirin is not guideline-recommended for AF stroke prevention in any current guideline (ESC, ACC/AHA, PERKI). The GP's prescription must be changed.

sections.body:
Typical atrial flutter is one of the most curable arrhythmias in cardiology — a single ablation procedure cures 95% of patients permanently. Recognising it on ECG, understanding why the rate is almost always 150 bpm, and knowing when it carries stroke risk are the core competencies.

## Typical atrial flutter

### The circuit

Typical atrial flutter is a macroreentrant circuit in the right atrium, rotating around the tricuspid annulus. The circuit passes through the cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) — the narrow strip of tissue between the tricuspid annulus and the inferior vena cava. This isthmus is the critical narrow passage — slow conduction here, fast conduction elsewhere in the circuit. The atrial rate is ~300 bpm (typical range 250–350 bpm).

Counter-clockwise flutter (typical, ~90%): wavefront passes through the CTI from right to left (when viewed from the front) → produces characteristic sawtooth flutter waves — negative (inverted) in leads II, III, aVF (descending sawtooth), positive in V1 (upright flutter waves in V1). Clockwise flutter (reverse typical, ~10%): opposite direction → positive flutter waves in inferior leads, inverted in V1.

### The ventricular rate — why it is usually 150 bpm

Atrial rate ≈ 300 bpm. The AV node cannot conduct 300 impulses per minute. Physiologically, it filters with a 2:1 block → every other atrial flutter wave conducts → ventricular rate = 300/2 = 150 bpm. This is the cardinal clue: regular tachycardia at exactly 150 bpm = flutter with 2:1 block until proven otherwise. If one flutter wave is buried in the QRS, the sawtooth may not be visible at first glance — adenosine (which increases AV block temporarily) or carotid massage will slow ventricular rate and reveal the flutter waves clearly.

Key concept: Regular tachycardia at 150 bpm = suspect atrial flutter with 2:1 block — look carefully at the baseline between QRS complexes for flutter waves
At 150 bpm with 2:1 flutter, one flutter wave falls within the QRS (buried). The other appears between QRS complexes. Without knowing to look, the baseline can appear flat. Clues: the "flat" baseline actually has a subtle undulation; the tachycardia is regular; the rate is exactly 150 (sinus tachycardia at exactly 150 is unusual). Give adenosine or perform carotid sinus massage — this will increase the degree of AV block transiently (2:1 → 4:1) → ventricular rate halves → flutter waves become unmistakable. This is a diagnostic manoeuvre, not a therapeutic one — flutter will resume when AV block resolves.

### Variable AV conduction in flutter

Flutter can conduct with variable block: 2:1 (rate ~150), 3:1 (rate ~100), 4:1 (rate ~75), or variable (irregular). Variable conduction can simulate irregular rhythm — but the flutter waves march through at a constant 300 bpm atrial rate.

### Stroke risk in flutter

Flutter carries similar embolic risk to AF (LA is not contracting effectively during flutter; LAA stasis → thrombus risk). Apply CHA₂DS₂-VASc and anticoagulate accordingly. The same cardioversion rules apply (≥3 weeks anticoagulation before elective cardioversion or TOE-guided).

### Ablation — the treatment of choice

Cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) ablation: creates a line of radiofrequency lesions from the tricuspid annulus to the IVC across the CTI → breaks the flutter circuit permanently. Success rate: 95%+. Recurrence rate: <5% (can occur if the ablation line reconnects or if atypical flutter circuits develop). One of the highest-yield ablation procedures in electrophysiology — strongly recommended over antiarrhythmic drug treatment for typical flutter.

Antidepressant drugs: beta-blockers or non-DHP CCBs for rate control, amiodarone or sotalol for rhythm control — less effective and have more side effects. Reserve for patients who decline ablation.

### Flutter + AF relationship

30–50% of flutter patients develop AF over 5 years. After CTI ablation for flutter, AF should still be monitored for and treated appropriately. The CTI ablation does not prevent AF (which is a different left atrial circuit).

## Focal atrial tachycardia — a reminder

Focal AT (covered in Chapter 5) arises from a specific ectopic focus in the atrium. Rate typically 150–250 bpm. Unlike flutter, the atrial rate is not fixed at 300 bpm. ECG clues: P wave morphology different from sinus (the shape tells you where the focus is), warm-up phenomenon (rate gradually increases at onset — unlike re-entrant tachycardia which starts suddenly), cool-down phenomenon (rate gradually slows at termination).

Localising the focus from P wave morphology:

- Negative P in aVL → left atrial origin (likely near PVs or left appendage)
- Positive P in all precordial leads → right atrial or crista terminalis focus
- Negative P in V1, positive in V6 → left atrial focus
- Positive P in V1 → right atrial focus

## Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT)

Defined by: rate >100 bpm, at least 3 different P wave morphologies in the same lead, irregular rhythm. The AV node is a bystander — it just conducts whatever comes. Mechanism: multiple enhanced automatic foci in the atrium, firing at different rates from different locations. Associated with: COPD (most common cause — hypoxia + catecholamines + sympathomimetic bronchodilators enhance automaticity), electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia), critical illness, theophylline toxicity.

Treatment: treat the underlying cause (COPD exacerbation, correct electrolytes, stop theophylline). Rate control with non-DHP CCBs (verapamil is most effective). Antiarrhythmic drugs are ineffective because the arrhythmia is triggered by the metabolic state, not a fixed circuit. Cardioversion is ineffective (multiple foci will restart immediately). Magnesium sulphate IV can suppress triggers.

Exam tip: MAT vs AF — these are frequently confused on exams because both are irregular tachycardias. The distinction is critical because cardioversion helps AF but does nothing for MAT, and MAT is a metabolic arrhythmia requiring cause correction rather than antiarrhythmic drug treatment. Key differences: MAT: irregular, but organised P waves present (≥3 morphologies, can see distinct P waves before each QRS)
AF: no organised P waves — only irregular fibrillatory baseline (f waves)
MAT: isoelectric baseline between P waves (unlike AF)
Clinical context: MAT = COPD/critical illness; AF = cardiac disease, hypertension, alcohol

Checkpoint: A 60-year-old with COPD exacerbation is on the medical ward. His ECG shows HR 130 bpm, irregular rhythm, at least 4 different P wave morphologies in lead II. His K⁺ is 2.9 mmol/L and Mg²⁺ is 0.6 mmol/L. He is on salbutamol nebs. The medical student suggests "DC cardioversion — it's AF." Why is this wrong, and what is the correct management?
This is multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT), not AF. The key distinguishing features: irregular tachycardia YES (both MAT and AF are irregular), but MAT has ≥3 distinct P wave morphologies visible before each QRS — organised P waves are present. AF has no organised P waves — only irregular fibrillatory baseline without distinguishable P waves. DC cardioversion is wrong for two reasons: (1) MAT has multiple enhanced automatic foci triggered by the metabolic environment (hypoxia, catecholamines, salbutamol, electrolyte abnormalities) — even if you cardiovert, the foci will immediately restart; (2) MAT is not a re-entrant circuit — cardioversion disrupts re-entry (by delivering a shock that simultaneously depolarises all myocardium), but it cannot stop automatic foci from firing again. Correct management: (1) treat the COPD exacerbation (oxygen, antibiotics, systemic steroids — the hypoxia and catecholamine excess are driving the automaticity); (2) correct K⁺ to ≥4.0 mmol/L and Mg²⁺ to >0.8 mmol/L; (3) consider reducing salbutamol dose or switching to ipratropium (salbutamol's β2-agonism increases cardiac automaticity); (4) if rate control needed: IV or oral verapamil. Do not cardiovert.

sections.body:
A wide complex tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise. The most dangerous error in acute arrhythmia management is misdiagnosing VT as SVT with aberrancy and giving verapamil — this can kill. This chapter builds the systematic approach to WCT diagnosis and the complete VT management algorithm.

## Wide complex tachycardia (WCT) — the differential

Any QRS ≥120 ms during tachycardia defines a wide complex tachycardia. Three possible causes:

1. Ventricular tachycardia (VT) — ~80% of all WCT in patients with structural heart disease
2. SVT with aberrant conduction — pre-existing BBB or rate-related BBB (when the tachycardia is faster than the refractory period of one bundle branch → functional BBB morphology)
3. Pre-excited tachycardia — antidromic AVRT or AF with WPW (accessory pathway conduction produces wide pre-excited QRS)

Warning: THE golden rule: treat every WCT as VT until proven otherwise. The consequences of misdiagnosing VT as SVT: giving verapamil or diltiazem → peripheral vasodilation (↓ SVR) + mild negative inotropy → haemodynamic collapse in a patient with a failing ventricle trying to compensate for VT. Cardioversion would have been safe. The consequences of treating SVT with aberrancy as VT: giving amiodarone, procainamide, or cardioverting → harmless (cardioversion of SVT → sinus rhythm). No harm done by over-treating toward VT. The asymmetry is critical: being wrong in the VT direction is safe; being wrong in the SVT direction can be fatal. When in doubt, treat as VT.

## ECG criteria for VT — Brugada algorithm and AV dissociation

AV dissociation is the most specific ECG finding for VT: independent P wave activity unrelated to the QRS complexes (atria and ventricles beating independently). Present in ~50% of VT — not always visible because P waves may be buried in QRS.

Other ECG features strongly favouring VT:

- Capture beats: occasional narrow QRS complexes within the wide complex tachycardia (a sinus impulse occasionally "captures" the ventricles via the normal His-Purkinje system before the VT circuit re-entrant wave arrives) — pathognomonic of AV dissociation
- Fusion beats: QRS morphology intermediate between sinus QRS and VT QRS (simultaneous activation from the VT circuit and a sinus impulse) — also pathognomonic of AV dissociation
- QRS duration >140 ms (in RBBB morphology) or >160 ms (in LBBB morphology) — wider than expected for aberrant SVT
- Extreme axis deviation (NW axis, "northwest" — negative in I, II, III, aVF) — uncommon in SVT with aberrancy
- Concordance in precordial leads: all precordial leads (V1–V6) either all positive (positive concordance) or all negative (negative concordance). In SVT with BBB, the precordial leads show a transition (R/S ratio changes). VT from the apex → all V leads positive; VT from the base → all V leads negative.
- Brugada sign: absence of an RS complex in any precordial lead (all leads are monophasic QS or R)

## VT classification

### By morphology

- Monomorphic VT: uniform, consistent QRS morphology → re-entrant mechanism around a fixed scar. Most common in ischaemic CMP post-MI. The QRS morphology is the "fingerprint" of the circuit — identifies exit site for ablation.
- Polymorphic VT: changing QRS morphology beat to beat → multiple re-entrant circuits or triggered activity. Causes: acute ischaemia (most common), QT prolongation (TdP), catecholamine excess (CPVT), structural disease. Polymorphic VT in the absence of QT prolongation = treat as acute ischaemia until proven otherwise.

### By substrate

- Scar-related (ischaemic) VT: most common. Scar from prior MI → slow conduction zones at the scar border → re-entry. Usually monomorphic. Target for catheter ablation.
- Idiopathic VT: structurally normal heart. RVOT-VT (right ventricular outflow tract VT) — most common idiopathic VT. Triggered activity (DAD mechanism — catecholamine-triggered cAMP-dependent Ca²⁺ release from the SR). LBBB morphology, inferior axis (QRS upright in II, III, aVF). Typically benign. Responds to adenosine (rare among VTs) and beta-blockers. Ablation curative (>90% success).
- Bundle branch re-entrant VT (BBRVT): re-entrant circuit using the right and left bundle branches. Rapid, haemodynamically poorly tolerated. Associated with dilated CMP. Wide QRS (usually LBBB morphology). Treated by ablation of the right bundle branch (cures the re-entry circuit).

## Acute management of VT

### Haemodynamically unstable VT (pulseless or BP <90 mmHg + altered consciousness)

→ Immediate synchronised cardioversion (if pulse present) or defibrillation (if pulseless VT → same as VF). Start at 200 J biphasic. If successful, address underlying cause.

### Haemodynamically stable monomorphic VT

Time to assess and attempt pharmacological cardioversion:

- IV amiodarone 150 mg over 10 min, then 1 mg/min infusion → drug of choice in structural heart disease. Terminates VT and prevents recurrence.
- IV procainamide 10–17 mg/kg over 30 min → blocks Na⁺ channels, effective for monomorphic VT. Also useful for pre-excited AF (unlike amiodarone which can enhance accessory pathway conduction).
- IV lidocaine 1–1.5 mg/kg bolus → less effective than amiodarone/procainamide for acute VT termination, but useful for VT in the context of acute MI (ischaemia-driven Na⁺-channel-dependent VT).
- Synchronised cardioversion if pharmacological therapy fails or haemodynamic status deteriorates

## VT storm (electrical storm)

Three or more episodes of VT/VF in 24 hours, or incessant VT, often despite antiarrhythmic drugs. Highly lethal. Management:

- Deep sedation (reduces sympathetic activation — the trigger for most VT storm)
- IV beta-blocker (IV metoprolol, esmolol) — suppress catecholamine-triggered VT
- IV amiodarone
- Consider general anaesthesia and intubation if unresponsive
- Urgent catheter VT ablation — ablation during VT storm significantly reduces recurrence and mortality (VANISH trial, SMASH-VT)
- IABP or MCS (Impella) if haemodynamically compromised

## Idiopathic RVOT-VT and the adenosine trick

RVOT-VT is the most important idiopathic VT to know. It originates from the RVOT (just below the pulmonary valve). Mechanism: DAD-triggered (cAMP-mediated Ca²⁺ overload from catecholamine stimulation → NCX activation → triggered beat). Therefore: it is triggered by catecholamines (exercise, stress), responds to adenosine (adenosine suppresses cAMP via A1 receptor) — rare among VTs! Also responds to beta-blockers and verapamil. ECG: LBBB morphology (right ventricular origin) + inferior axis (positive in II, III, aVF — the activation spreads inferiorly from the RVOT to the ventricular apex). Often exercise-induced or stress-induced.

Checkpoint: A 65-year-old with ischaemic CMP (EF 30%, prior anterior MI) is brought in with regular wide complex tachycardia at 185 bpm. His BP is 95/60. The ECG shows QRS 160 ms, RBBB morphology, extreme northwest axis (negative in I, II, III), no visible P waves. He is conscious but very dizzy. The nurse asks: "Should I give verapamil?" What do you do next and what do you say?
No verapamil — this is VT. This is a wide complex tachycardia in a patient with confirmed structural heart disease (ischaemic CMP, prior anterior MI) — statistically VT with overwhelming probability (~95%). The ECG features confirm VT: QRS 160 ms (very wide), extreme northwest axis (negative in I, II, III — strongly against SVT with aberrancy, which produces a typical RBBB axis), no visible P waves (AV dissociation possible), prior structural heart disease. Verapamil would cause vasodilation and negative inotropy in a patient whose heart is already trying to compensate for VT at BP 95/60 → haemodynamic collapse → cardiac arrest. The patient is haemodynamically compromised (BP 95, dizzy) but conscious. Action: immediate synchronised DC cardioversion — 200 J biphasic. Conscious patient → brief sedation (IV midazolam 2–5 mg or IV propofol) before cardioversion. Do not delay with pharmacological options given BP 95. After cardioversion: IV amiodarone infusion to prevent recurrence, urgent cardiology/EP review for ICD implantation planning, and VT ablation discussion if recurrent.

sections.body:
Sudden cardiac death (SCD) kills 5–7 million people globally each year. Most are preventable. Understanding who is at risk, how to risk-stratify them, and what interventions actually reduce mortality separates evidence-based practice from educated guessing.

## Definitions

- Ventricular fibrillation (VF): completely disorganised ventricular electrical activity — no coordinated mechanical contraction, no cardiac output. Fatal within minutes without CPR + defibrillation.
- Sudden cardiac death (SCD): unexpected death from cardiac cause within 1 hour of symptom onset (or within 24 hours of being seen alive if unwitnessed). Most cases: VF (75–80%), VT degenerating to VF (~15%), pulseless electromechanical dissociation (PEA, ~5%). SCD from bradycardia/asystole ~5%.
- Sudden cardiac arrest (SCA): cardiac arrest where resuscitation was attempted (may or may not survive to hospital discharge). SCD refers to those who die.
- Aborted SCD: survived SCA (typically after CPR + defibrillation). These patients are at very high risk of recurrence — secondary prevention ICD is indicated.

## Causes of SCD — by age group

Age group | Most common causes | Key investigation
<35 years | HCM (most common), ARVC, CPVT, LQTS, Brugada syndrome, commotio cordis, anomalous coronary arteries, myocarditis | CMR, genetic testing, EP study
35–60 years | Ischaemic CMP (most common), HCM, ARVC, dilated CMP, idiopathic VF | Coronary angiography, echo, CMR, EP study
>60 years | Ischaemic CMP (dominant), degenerative conduction disease, advanced HF | Coronary angiography, echo

## Risk stratification for primary prevention ICD

Covered in the HF Deep Dive (Chapter 7) and ACS Deep Dive — key points here:

- EF ≤35% is the dominant risk marker for SCD risk in structural heart disease. MADIT-II, SCD-HeFT, DANISH trials establish this threshold.
- Post-MI timing: ICD benefit is established ≥40 days after MI. The early post-MI period has high VF risk but ICD does not improve outcome (DINAMIT, IRIS — revascularisation and medications address the acuteischaemic substrate more effectively).
- Genetics-based risk stratification: LMNA mutation → ICD at EF ≤45%; HCM → HCM Risk-SCD calculator; ARVC → high-risk features (sustained VT, severe RV dysfunction, TMEM43 mutation).
- Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) on CMR: increasing evidence that the amount and pattern of LGE (fibrosis) is an independent predictor of VT/SCD beyond EF alone — patients with significant LGE but EF 36–49% may still be at high SCD risk.

## Secondary prevention ICD

After survived cardiac arrest (VF or haemodynamically unstable VT) not due to a reversible cause: ICD is indicated without waiting for any EF threshold. The evidence: AVID, CIDS, CASH trials — ICD reduces mortality vs antiarrhythmic drugs (primarily amiodarone) in secondary prevention. Amiodarone is not a substitute for ICD in secondary prevention.

## Advanced life support — VF/pulseless VT algorithm

CPR quality is the most important determinant of outcome — every minute without CPR = 10% decrease in survival. Defibrillation within 3–5 minutes = 50–70% survival to hospital discharge. After 10 minutes without CPR: survival <1%.

1. Confirm unresponsive + no breathing → call for help + AED
2. Start high-quality CPR: 30 compressions (rate 100–120/min, depth 5–6 cm, full recoil) : 2 breaths. Minimise interruptions (<5 seconds for rhythm check).
3. Attach defibrillator → assess rhythm
4. Shockable (VF/pulseless VT): defibrillate 200 J biphasic → immediately resume CPR for 2 minutes → check rhythm → if still shockable → defibrillate → CPR 2 min → check → adrenaline (epinephrine) 1 mg IV after 3rd shock and every 3–5 minutes → amiodarone 300 mg IV after 3rd shock (then 150 mg after 5th shock)
5. Non-shockable (PEA/asystole): continue CPR, adrenaline 1 mg IV every 3–5 min, find and treat reversible causes (4Hs + 4Ts: Hypoxia, Hypovolaemia, Hypo/Hyperkalaemia, Hypothermia; Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombosis)

Exam tip: Post-resuscitation care — the temperature controversy resolved: Post-cardiac arrest syndrome causes hypoxic brain injury, myocardial stunning, and systemic ischaemia-reperfusion injury. Targeted temperature management (TTM) at 33–36°C was standard for years (HACA trial 2002, Bernard 2002). The TTM2 trial (2021) showed no benefit of 33°C vs normothermia (37.8°C) with strict fever prevention. Current recommendation (ESC 2021 cardiac arrest guidelines): prevent fever strictly (target <37.7°C) in all comatose post-arrest patients. Active cooling to 33°C is no longer routinely required but may be considered in selected patients. Coronary angiography: immediate for STEMI post-arrest; selective (not immediate) for non-STEMI arrest (COACT, TOMAHAWK trials — immediate angio did not improve outcomes in out-of-hospital arrest without STEMI).

Checkpoint: A 45-year-old jogger collapses on the running track. A bystander starts CPR. Paramedics arrive at 6 minutes, find VF on the defibrillator, and shock 200 J → rhythm converts to sinus at 88 bpm. BP 92/58. He is intubated and transferred to your CCU. ECG post-ROSC: ST elevation in leads I, aVL, V5–V6. What are the three immediate priorities in post-resuscitation care?
1. Urgent coronary angiography ± PCI — ECG shows lateral STEMI (ST elevation I, aVL, V5–V6 = LCx territory). This is an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with STEMI on post-ROSC ECG. Immediate coronary angiography and primary PCI is indicated (STEMI post-arrest = Level I indication). This is the likely cause of the VF (acute ischaemia → VF). Reperfusion is both life-saving and neuroprotective (restores coronary perfusion to the stunned myocardium). 2. Temperature management and fever prevention — he is comatose post-arrest. Target normothermia ≤37.7°C, prevent fever (fever worsens neurological outcomes). Active cooling to 33°C is not routinely indicated (TTM2 trial), but paracetamol + cooling blanket to maintain normothermia is standard. 3. Haemodynamic support — BP 92/58 indicates post-arrest cardiogenic shock (combination of stunned myocardium + ischaemia from STEMI). IV norepinephrine to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg. Consider IABP or Impella if haemodynamics don't improve after PCI. Reassess EF at 90 days for ICD decision (primary VF post-STEMI may not require ICD if EF recovers).

sections.body:
Every valve lesion can be understood as either an obstruction (stenosis) or a leak (regurgitation). These create two fundamentally different haemodynamic insults — pressure overload and volume overload — that the heart responds to in completely different ways, with completely different long-term consequences.

## Stenosis versus regurgitation — the core distinction

Stenosis — pressure overload: A narrowed valve forces the upstream chamber to generate higher pressure to push blood through. The upstream chamber hypertrophies concentrically (sarcomeres in parallel → wall thickens without chamber dilation) to normalise wall stress by the Law of Laplace. The ventricle works against increased resistance with each beat. Examples: aortic stenosis (LV pressure overload), mitral stenosis (LA pressure overload), pulmonary stenosis (RV pressure overload).

Regurgitation — volume overload: An incompetent valve allows blood to flow backwards, forcing the upstream chamber to handle the normal volume plus the regurgitant fraction every beat. The chamber dilates eccentrically (sarcomeres in series → longer myocytes → larger chamber without proportional wall thickening). The ventricle pumps a larger total stroke volume to maintain forward output. Examples: aortic regurgitation (LV volume overload), mitral regurgitation (LV + LA volume overload).

## The pressure-volume loop — reading ventricular mechanics

The pressure-volume (PV) loop traces the cardiac cycle as LV pressure (y-axis) vs LV volume (x-axis). Four phases form the loop:

1. Isovolumetric contraction: mitral valve closes, aortic valve not yet open → pressure rises, volume unchanged (vertical left limb)
2. Ejection: aortic valve opens → LV ejects blood, volume falls, pressure rises then falls (upper limb)
3. Isovolumetric relaxation: aortic valve closes, mitral not yet open → pressure falls, volume unchanged (vertical right limb)
4. Diastolic filling: mitral valve opens → LV fills, pressure rises slightly, volume increases (lower limb)

### How valve lesions deform the PV loop

- Aortic stenosis: the upper limb is shifted upward and to the right (higher systolic pressure needed, larger end-diastolic volume from hypertrophy). The loop is tall and narrow → high pressure work, small volume change. Stroke volume is preserved until late.
- Aortic regurgitation: loop is shifted rightward (larger EDV from volume overload) and the lower left boundary is widened (no true isovolumetric relaxation — blood immediately starts entering through the regurgitant AV before the MV opens). Loop is wide and tall → high volume work at high pressure.
- Mitral regurgitation: loop shifts left (lower afterload — LV can eject into both the aorta and the LA). EF appears high (falsely reassuring) because some ejection goes backwards into the low-resistance LA. This is a critical concept — a "normal" EF in severe MR is actually reduced myocardial function.

Key concept: In severe mitral regurgitation, a "preserved" EF of 60% may represent significant LV dysfunction — the easy ejection into the low-pressure LA masks early contractile failure
The LV in severe MR has two outlets during systole: the aorta (high impedance) and the regurgitant LA (low impedance). Blood preferentially flows into the low-resistance LA → the LV appears to have excellent ejection. EF is inflated compared to an equivalent degree of myocardial damage in, say, ischaemic CMP. As a result: surgery is indicated in primary MR when EF falls to ≤60% or LVESD reaches ≥40 mm — these thresholds are deliberately strict because at "normal" EF 55% in MR, the true myocardial function may already be compromised. By contrast, in aortic stenosis or HFrEF, EF ≤50% triggers intervention. MR gets a tighter threshold.

## The Gorlin formula and valve area

The Gorlin formula estimates valve area from invasive haemodynamic measurements:

Equation: Valve Area (cm²) = Cardiac Output / (44.3 × Heart Rate × Systolic Ejection Period × √Mean Pressure Gradient)

In practice, invasive measurement is rarely needed for isolated stenotic lesions — echocardiographic calculation of valve area using the continuity equation (for AS) or the pressure half-time method (for MS) is standard. However, understanding the formula reveals an important clinical trap:

Key concept: Low cardiac output reduces the pressure gradient across a stenotic valve — masking its true severity
In a patient with severe AS and reduced cardiac output (from HFrEF or low-flow states): the gradient across the valve is flow-dependent. Less flow → smaller gradient. You may measure a mean gradient of only 20–30 mmHg in a patient with truly severe AS because the ventricle is too weak to generate a high gradient. This is the "low-flow low-gradient AS" trap — Chapter 13 covers this in full. Never diagnose AS severity from the gradient alone — always calculate valve area (AVA). Severe AS is defined by AVA <1.0 cm² regardless of gradient.

## Compensatory mechanisms — and why they eventually fail

### Pressure overload (stenosis)

Concentric hypertrophy maintains wall stress and preserves systolic function. But the hypertrophied, stiff LV develops diastolic dysfunction → elevated filling pressures → dyspnoea. Eventually, as the obstruction worsens and coronary reserve is exhausted: subendocardial ischaemia, myocyte death, fibrosis → transition from compensated concentric hypertrophy to HFpEF → then HFrEF. Symptoms appear when compensation fails — explaining why AS is silent for decades and then deteriorates rapidly.

### Volume overload (regurgitation)

Eccentric dilation maintains forward stroke volume (by the Frank-Starling mechanism — larger EDV → larger SV). But progressive dilation → wall stress rises by Laplace → LV must hypertrophy to normalise stress → eccentric hypertrophy → eventually LV dilation outpaces hypertrophy → wall stress exceeds compensation → irreversible LV dysfunction. The transition from compensated to decompensated regurgitation is often insidious — which is why serial echo surveillance is essential.

Mental model: Think of stenosis as trying to squeeze toothpaste through a narrow cap. The tube (ventricle) has to build stronger walls to generate the pressure to push through. Think of regurgitation as a leaky syringe — you have to push twice as much fluid through the plunger to get the same amount out the front, because half leaks back. The body accommodates both initially, but neither can be sustained without eventually damaging the pump. The key insight: fix the valve before the pump is permanently damaged. Timing of intervention is the central challenge in valvular disease.

## Natural history — the three general rules

1. Stenosis progresses relentlessly: the natural history of all stenotic lesions is progressive narrowing — calcification, fibrosis, and flow restriction worsen inexorably. Intervention timing is about identifying the threshold where the risk of the valve lesion exceeds the risk of the procedure.
2. Regurgitation is initially well tolerated, then irreversible: the volume-overloaded heart compensates for years to decades. But once decompensation begins, LV dysfunction may become irreversible even after valve repair — hence the importance of intervention before EF falls.
3. Symptoms herald decompensation — but asymptomatic disease can still cause damage: waiting for symptoms before acting costs myocardial reserve. Modern guidelines increasingly recommend intervention in asymptomatic patients when objective evidence of LV strain appears.

Checkpoint: A 55-year-old woman has severe chronic aortic regurgitation. Her EF is 62%, LVESD is 44 mm. She is NYHA Class I (no symptoms). Her cardiologist suggests "watchful waiting since she has no symptoms." Is this correct, and what thresholds would trigger intervention?
This management is not optimal. The LVESD of 44 mm has crossed the surgical threshold for severe AR. ESC 2021 guidelines for severe AR intervention: surgery is indicated (Class I) when: (1) symptomatic (any NYHA class), OR (2) asymptomatic but EF ≤50%, OR (3) asymptomatic but LVESD >50 mm (or >25 mm/m² BSA in smaller patients), OR (4) undergoing other cardiac surgery. Additionally, many current guidelines (ACC/AHA 2021) now recommend considering surgery in asymptomatic severe AR with progressive LV dilation: LVESD >50 mm. At LVESD 44 mm she is approaching but has not yet crossed the classic ESC threshold of 50 mm — however, she has crossed the ACC/AHA 2021 threshold of ≥50 mm borderline. The trajectory matters: is LVESD growing on serial echo? The most important point: do not wait for symptoms alone. LVESD ≥50 mm is a class I indication for surgery regardless of symptoms. At 44 mm: schedule 6-monthly echo surveillance and intervene when LVESD reaches 50 mm or if EF falls below 50%.

sections.body:
Every replaced valve trades the problems of the diseased native valve for a new set of prosthesis-specific complications. The choice between mechanical and biological valves, and the management of those complications, is one of the most frequently tested areas in cardiology examinations.

## Mechanical vs biological valves — the core trade-off

Mechanical valves: • Indefinite durability — last a lifetime, no re-operation for structural failure
• Require lifelong warfarin anticoagulation (INR 2.5–3.5 for mitral, 2.0–3.0 for aortic)
• Thromboembolism risk even on anticoagulation: ~1–2%/year
• Major bleeding risk from anticoagulation: ~1–2%/year
• Audible click (can disturb patient and partner)
• Contraindicated in patients unable to comply with anticoagulation
• Preferred in: age <60 (younger patients justify the anticoagulation burden to avoid re-operation)

Biological valves (bioprostheses): • No lifelong anticoagulation (warfarin 3 months post-implant for aortic; 3 months for mitral then aspirin)
• Progressive structural valve deterioration (SVD) — typical longevity 10–20 years
• SVD risk higher in younger patients (faster calcification in metabolically active younger tissue)
• Re-operation for SVD anticipated — but "valve-in-valve" TAVR can treat failed surgical bioprosthesis without re-operation
• Preferred in: age >65–70 (less likely to outlive the valve), patients unable to take anticoagulation, women of childbearing potential (avoid warfarin in pregnancy)

Key concept: The age threshold for mechanical vs biological valve choice has shifted toward biological valves — primarily because transcatheter valve-in-valve procedures can now extend biological valve longevity without re-operation
Historically the rule was: <60 years → mechanical; >65 years → biological. The emergence of valve-in-valve TAVR (deploying a transcatheter valve within a failed surgical bioprosthesis) has changed the calculus. A 55-year-old receiving a surgical bioprosthesis today knows that when the valve fails in 15–20 years (at age 70–75), it can likely be treated with a transcatheter procedure rather than a third sternotomy. Combined with the significant quality-of-life burden of warfarin monitoring, this has shifted many guidelines and heart teams toward discussing biological valves in younger patients. The current recommendation: individualised shared decision-making. Patient lifestyle, anticoagulation compliance, and preferences should drive the decision at any age between 60–65 years.

## Anticoagulation for prosthetic valves

Valve type and position | Target INR | Additional antiplatelet?
Mechanical aortic valve — low risk (bileaflet, normal function, no other risk factors) | 2.0–3.0 | Low-dose aspirin 75–100 mg OD (Class IIa)
Mechanical aortic valve — high risk (prior thromboembolism, AF, LV dysfunction, older valve types) | 2.5–3.5 | Aspirin 75–100 mg OD
Mechanical mitral valve | 2.5–3.5 | Aspirin 75–100 mg OD
Mechanical tricuspid valve | 3.0 (higher due to low-flow right heart) | Aspirin OD
Biological aortic valve (surgical) | 2.0–3.0 for first 3 months, then stop warfarin if sinus rhythm | Aspirin 75–100 mg indefinitely
TAVR | Not routinely anticoagulated unless another indication (AF, LV thrombus, etc.) | Aspirin + clopidogrel for 3 months, then aspirin alone (POPULAR-TAVI trial)

Warning: DOACs are NOT used in patients with mechanical heart valves — warfarin only. The RE-ALIGN trial (dabigatran vs warfarin in mechanical valves) was stopped early due to excess thromboembolic events and bleeding in the dabigatran arm. Direct oral anticoagulants do not adequately prevent mechanical valve thrombosis. This applies to all DOACs (dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban). Exception where DOACs ARE used: AF in patients with biological valves or native valve disease (including MS without mechanical valve) — DOACs are standard for the AF indication but do not prevent mechanical valve thrombosis.

## Prosthetic valve complications

### Structural valve deterioration (SVD)

Calcification and leaflet degeneration of biological valves. Defined by: severe haemodynamic deterioration (mean gradient ≥40 mmHg for aortic), or severe regurgitation on echo. Treatment: re-operation (SAVR) or valve-in-valve TAVR (preferred in high surgical risk re-operations).

### Prosthetic valve thrombosis (PVT)

Thrombus formation on the mechanical valve leaflets — presents with sudden haemodynamic compromise, new murmur, or abnormal valve motion (cinefluoroscopy shows restricted disc motion). Divided by haemodynamic impact: obstructive PVT (high gradient, reduced leaflet excursion) vs non-obstructive PVT (no obstruction, incidental echo finding). Treatment: obstructive PVT with haemodynamic compromise → emergency surgery or IV thrombolytics (tPA). Non-obstructive PVT → IV heparin intensification, then optimise INR.

### Prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE)

Early PVE (<1 year post-surgery): S. epidermidis, S. aureus, Gram-negative organisms — coagulase-negative staphylococci dominate. Biofilm formation makes it very difficult to eradicate with antibiotics alone — surgery almost always required. Late PVE (>1 year): similar organisms to native valve IE (viridans streptococci, S. aureus). TOE is mandatory — assess for perivalvular abscess (very common in aortic PVE).

### Patient-prosthesis mismatch (PPM)

The implanted valve has an effective orifice area too small for the patient's body surface area → high residual transvalvular gradient even with a "normal" prosthesis. Defined by indexed EOA (iEOA = EOA / BSA): iEOA <0.85 cm²/m² = moderate PPM; <0.65 cm²/m² = severe PPM. Severe PPM: worse outcomes post-AVR. Prevention: choose the correct prosthesis size for BSA; consider aortic annulus enlargement at surgery if native annulus is small; biological valves generally have better EOA than mechanical valves of the same ring size.

Checkpoint: A 50-year-old man with a mechanical mitral valve (St Jude Medical, bileaflet, implanted 8 years ago) presents to A&E with acute onset severe dyspnoea and hypotension (BP 75/50 mmHg, HR 115 bpm). His INR on admission is 1.5 (target 2.5–3.5 — subtherapeutic). TOE: severely restricted posterior disc motion, mean gradient 28 mmHg (previously 4 mmHg), large thrombus mass. What is the diagnosis and the two management options?
Obstructive mechanical mitral valve thrombosis — a life-threatening emergency. The diagnosis is confirmed by: clinical haemodynamic collapse + TOE showing restricted disc motion + markedly elevated gradient + visible thrombus. The subtherapeutic INR (1.5) is the precipitating cause. Two management options: 1. Emergency surgery (mechanical valve re-replacement or thrombectomy): the definitive treatment. Preferred when: large thrombus, haemodynamically unstable despite resuscitation, recent neurological event (thrombolysis risk), centre with surgical experience. Mortality from emergency re-operation for PVT is 10–15% — significant, but lower than the alternative. 2. IV thrombolytic therapy (tPA): alteplase 10 mg IV bolus then 90 mg over 90 minutes (or slow infusion protocols). Consider when: no neurosurgical backup, patient too unstable for surgery, no recent ICH or stroke (major contraindication), no large thrombus (<0.8 cm²). Success rate: 60–80% for restoration of valve function. Risks: systemic embolism from thrombus fragmentation (stroke in ~10–20%), recurrent thrombosis. If thrombolysis is chosen: heparin infusion after tPA, target INR optimisation, and close follow-up (repeat TOE at 24h). The choice between surgery and thrombolysis requires rapid heart team discussion. At a tertiary centre with available cardiac surgery → surgery is generally preferred for obstructive PVT with haemodynamic compromise. In a non-surgical centre → thrombolysis as a bridge to transfer or definitive treatment.

sections.body:
The transcatheter revolution has transformed valvular heart disease from an exclusively surgical field into a discipline where most patients can now be treated through a groin puncture. Understanding TAVR patient selection, the procedure, and its specific complications is essential for every modern cardiologist.

## TAVR — principles and evolution

Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR, also called TAVI — transcatheter aortic valve implantation) deploys a collapsible bioprosthetic valve via catheter, typically through the femoral artery (transfemoral approach, ~95% of cases). The valve is crimped onto a delivery catheter, advanced under fluoroscopic + echo guidance, and expanded at the native aortic annulus — either by balloon inflation (balloon-expandable valves: Edwards SAPIEN 3/Ultra) or by self-expanding nitinol frame (Medtronic Evolut R/Pro, Boston Scientific Acurate). The native diseased valve is pushed aside rather than removed.

### Trial evidence — expansion across risk categories

- PARTNER 1 (2011): inoperable patients — TAVR vs medical management (balloon aortic valvuloplasty). TAVR dramatically reduced mortality (20% absolute risk reduction at 1 year). Opened the field.
- PARTNER 1B / CoreValve High Risk (2012–2014): high surgical risk — TAVR non-inferior to SAVR.
- PARTNER 2 / SURTAVI (2016–2017): intermediate risk — TAVR non-inferior to SAVR.
- PARTNER 3 / Evolut Low Risk (2019): low surgical risk — TAVR non-inferior to SAVR at 2 years for SAPIEN 3; Evolut showed superiority for the composite at 1 year. TAVR now approved for low-risk patients.

Current state: TAVR is the dominant treatment modality for severe AS across all risk categories at most high-volume centres. In 2023, more TAVR than SAVR procedures were performed in the USA.

## Patient selection for TAVR vs SAVR

The heart team must individualise the decision. TAVR is preferred when:

- Age ≥75 years (TAVR longevity concerns less relevant; surgical risk increases with age)
- High or intermediate surgical risk (STS ≥4% or EuroSCORE II ≥4%)
- Frailty, prior sternotomy (hostile chest), severe COPD, severe CKD making surgical risk prohibitive
- Patient preference for the less invasive approach and faster recovery

SAVR is preferred when:

- Age <60 years — longer durability of mechanical valve or concern about TAVR valve longevity
- Anatomical factors unfavourable for TAVR: severe aorto-iliac disease (no transfemoral access), very small or very large annulus, severely bicuspid valve with complex anatomy (relative — experienced TAVR centres now treat bicuspid AS)
- Concurrent disease requiring open surgery: CABG, other valve surgery
- Low surgical risk + young patient — SAVR offers established long-term data

## Pre-TAVR workup

- CT aortogram: essential — measures aortic annulus dimensions (determines valve size), assesses iliofemoral access (calcification, diameter ≥5.5 mm needed for most systems), evaluates coronary ostia height (TAVR leaflets may block coronary access — coronary occlusion is a rare but catastrophic complication)
- Echocardiography: confirms AS severity, evaluates other valves, LV function
- Coronary angiography: evaluate and treat significant CAD before or at TAVR
- Frailty assessment: gait speed, grip strength, KATZ ADL, cognitive function — frailty significantly predicts post-TAVR outcomes

## TAVR complications

Complication | Frequency | Mechanism / management
Permanent pacemaker requirement | 10–25% (self-expanding); 5–10% (balloon-expandable) | Valve frame compresses the AV node and LBBB bundle → complete heart block. New LBBB post-TAVR → monitor 48–72h. PPM if complete heart block persists >24–48h.
Paravalvular regurgitation (PVR) | Mild: 15–25%; Moderate-severe: <5% with modern valves | Incomplete sealing between the valve frame and the calcified annulus → regurgitation around the valve. Mild PVR: tolerated. Moderate-severe PVR: associated with excess mortality — consider post-dilation, snare technique, or re-implantation.
Stroke | 1–4% | Debris embolisation from calcified leaflets during manipulation. Embolic protection devices (Sentinel) reduce stroke burden by capturing debris. Routine use debated.
Coronary occlusion | <1% (1–2% in bicuspid) | Valve leaflets displaced toward coronary ostia → obstruction. CT planning critical. Can be treated with TAVI-in-TAVI or coronary stenting. Emergency bailout with coronary stent or bypass.
Vascular access complications | 3–7% | Femoral artery haematoma, dissection, pseudoaneurysm. Reduced with smaller delivery systems and ultrasound-guided access.
Valve thrombosis | Subclinical: ~15%; clinical: <1% | Subclinical leaflet thrombosis on CT (hypo-attenuating leaflet thickening — HALT). Often resolves with anticoagulation. Consequence of clinical valve thrombosis: valve degeneration, stroke.

## Transcatheter mitral and tricuspid interventions

- MitraClip (TEER): covered in Chapter 6 — the established transcatheter MR treatment based on COAPT trial criteria.
- Transcatheter mitral valve replacement (TMVR): several devices under investigation (Tendyne, Tiara, Intrepid). More anatomically challenging than TAVR — the mitral annulus is larger, non-circular, and lacks calcium to anchor devices. No large RCTs yet; registry data emerging.
- Transcatheter tricuspid repair/replacement: TriClip (TRILUMINATE), CLASP TR (PASCAL), EVOQUE (TRISCEND II). Rapidly evolving — significant TR reduction, improved functional class, reduced HF hospitalisations in pivotal trials. No mortality RCT data yet.
- Balloon mitral valvuloplasty (BMV/PTMC): covered in Chapter 5 — the gold standard for rheumatic MS with favourable anatomy.
- Valve-in-valve TAVR: deploying a transcatheter valve within a failed surgical bioprosthesis — the most important "second procedure" for bioprosthesis failure. Avoids re-sternotomy. Results are generally good but LVOTO risk (small surgical bioprosthesis + TAVR frame → coronary obstruction) requires careful CT planning. BASILICA technique (bioprosthetic or native aortic valve laceration to prevent LVOTO) is used in high-risk anatomy.

Checkpoint: A 72-year-old man with severe symptomatic AS (AVA 0.8 cm², mean gradient 48 mmHg) also has moderate CAD (70% proximal LAD stenosis). Heart team discussion is requested. How does the concurrent CAD affect the TAVR vs SAVR decision, and in what order should the two conditions be treated?
Concurrent significant CAD (≥70% proximal LAD) complicates the decision but does not change the overall treatment indication for AS — AVR is still required. The question is which procedure first and which approach. Heart team considerations: If SAVR is chosen: CABG (LAD bypass) can be performed simultaneously at the same sternotomy — one operation addresses both problems. This is the historical "combined CABG + AVR" — well-established, slightly higher surgical risk than isolated CABG or isolated SAVR alone, but avoids two separate procedures. If TAVR is chosen: PCI of the proximal LAD should generally be performed before TAVR. The reasons: (1) during TAVR, haemodynamic instability (transient rapid pacing for balloon expansion) + periprocedural hypotension may be poorly tolerated with an unrevascularised 70% LAD; (2) post-TAVR, coronary access may be more difficult (TAVR leaflets near coronary ostia). PCI first → staged TAVR 1–4 weeks later is standard practice. At 72 years with intermediate surgical risk (STS likely 3–5% based on age and comorbidities): TAVR with staged PCI is a reasonable and increasingly common approach, avoiding sternotomy. However, some patients at this age with good surgical fitness and preference for the combined one-operation approach may prefer CABG + SAVR. Heart team input and patient preference are essential. This exemplifies why the Heart Team model (interventional cardiologist + cardiac surgeon + imaging + cardiologist) is a Class I recommendation — not just a box to tick.
