title: Secondary prevention after ACS and stroke

sections.body:
The heart and the mind are not separate systems. Depression, anxiety, chronic psychosocial stress, and burnout are independent cardiovascular risk factors with effect sizes comparable to traditional risk factors — and they are the most undertreated risk factors in all of preventive cardiology.

## Depression and cardiovascular disease — a bidirectional relationship

Depression is both a consequence and a cause of cardiovascular disease. The relationship operates in both directions:

- Depression → CVD: major depression doubles the risk of incident MI. Post-MI depression is present in 20–30% of patients and independently predicts recurrent MI, HF hospitalisation, and mortality (hazard ratio ~2.0 for cardiac mortality). Depression impairs adherence to medications, reduces physical activity, and drives smoking and poor diet.
- CVD → Depression: MI, HF diagnosis, implantation of ICD, diagnosis of severe valvular disease — all trigger depression and anxiety. The physical limitation of heart failure (fatigue, dyspnoea) creates a powerful psychological burden.
- Shared mechanisms: inflammation (elevated CRP, IL-6, TNF-α in depression — the same inflammatory mediators drive atherosclerosis); HPA axis dysregulation → excess cortisol → hypertension, visceral obesity, insulin resistance; autonomic dysfunction (↑ sympathetic, ↓ vagal tone) → ventricular arrhythmia susceptibility and impaired HR variability; platelet hyperreactivity in depression → prothrombotic state.

## Psychosocial risk factors — the evidence

Factor | Relative risk for CVD | Mechanism
Major depression | 1.8–2.0× incident CHD; 2.0× post-MI mortality | Sympathoadrenal activation, inflammation, platelet hyperactivity, poor self-care
Anxiety disorders | 1.3–1.5× incident CVD; higher in panic disorder | Sympathetic activation, episodic tachycardia and BP spikes, hyperventilation-induced coronary spasm
Chronic work stress / job strain | 1.3–1.5× CVD (INTERHEART study) | Sustained HPA activation, poor sleep, reduced recovery time
Social isolation / loneliness | 1.3× CVD mortality (meta-analysis, 300,000 patients) | Reduced social buffering of stress; lower adherence; inflammatory activation
Type D personality (negative affect + social inhibition) | 2–4× adverse cardiac outcomes in patients with CHD | Suppressed emotional expression → chronic sympathetic activation; avoided healthcare
PTSD | 1.5–2× incident CVD; especially in women and veterans | Hypervigilance → chronic sympathetic activation; sleep disruption; substance use

## Screening tools

- PHQ-2 (Patient Health Questionnaire-2): two questions ("Over the past 2 weeks, have you felt down, depressed, or hopeless?" and "Have you had little interest or pleasure in doing things?") — score ≥3 → full PHQ-9. Validated screening tool recommended at every post-ACS follow-up visit.
- PHQ-9: 9-item depression scale; score ≥10 = moderate depression → treatment consideration; score ≥20 = severe.
- GAD-7: generalised anxiety disorder scale. Score ≥8 = moderate anxiety.
- DASS-21: depression, anxiety, and stress scale — validated in Indonesian population; widely used in research and clinical settings in Indonesia.

## Treatment of depression in cardiac patients — what is safe?

- Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT): first-line; no cardiac side effects. ENRICHD trial: CBT improved depression post-MI but did not significantly reduce mortality (underpowered for this endpoint). Cardiac rehabilitation that incorporates psychological support improves both depression scores and exercise capacity.
- SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram): first-line pharmacological treatment in cardiac patients. SADHART trial: sertraline safe and effective post-ACS depression. SSRI-mediated serotonin reuptake inhibition also reduces platelet activation (an antiplatelet effect — generally beneficial in CHD patients). QTc effect: most SSRIs have minimal QTc prolongation; citalopram and escitalopram at high doses (citalopram >40 mg; escitalopram >20 mg) can prolong QTc — use caution in patients at risk for TdP.
- Avoid in cardiac patients: Tricyclic antidepressants (TCA — amitriptyline, imipramine): prolong QTc, sodium channel blockade (Ic-like effects), orthostatic hypotension — multiple cardiac adverse effects. Only use if no alternative available. SNRIs (venlafaxine): raises BP and HR — caution in poorly-controlled HTN and tachyarrhythmias.

## Burnout and chronic occupational stress — the physician's own risk

Clinical link: A chapter on mental health and CV risk would be incomplete without acknowledging that physicians — particularly those in demanding specialties like cardiology and critical care — are at significantly elevated risk of burnout, depression, and premature cardiovascular events from occupational stress. Indonesian medical residents and junior physicians face specific structural stressors: long working hours, inadequate sleep, high patient-to-physician ratios, financial pressure, and a culture that historically valorises stoicism over help-seeking. The research on physician CV risk is unequivocal: night shifts → increased MI and stroke risk; sleep deprivation → hypertension, insulin resistance, and systemic inflammation; chronic unprocessed work-related grief → depression and social isolation. Recognising and addressing these risk factors in oneself is not weakness — it is preventive cardiology at the most immediate scale available.

Checkpoint: A 52-year-old bank manager, 3 months post-MI and PCI, comes to your clinic. He is on all correct secondary prevention medications, LDL-C 1.5 mmol/L, BP 124/78 mmHg. His wife says he has been "different since the heart attack — withdrawn, not interested in anything, not sleeping." He dismisses concerns: "I'm fine, just tired from recovery." His PHQ-2 score is 4 out of 6. How do you proceed?
PHQ-2 score 4 = positive screen for depression → administer full PHQ-9. Post-MI depression is present in 20–30% of post-MI patients, doubles his risk of recurrent MI and cardiac mortality, impairs medication adherence, and worsens his quality of life. His dismissal ("just tired") is classic male under-reporting of emotional distress in Indonesian culture — the physician must gently but firmly persist. Frame it clinically: "The heart attack affects the mind as well as the heart — this is a very common medical response to what you've been through, and it needs treatment just like your other risk factors." If PHQ-9 ≥10 (moderate depression): (1) Start sertraline 50 mg OD (SADHART-proven safe post-ACS, titrate to 100–200 mg). No significant QTc concern at standard doses. Explain it takes 4–6 weeks to see full effect. (2) Refer for CBT or psychologist input — ideally integrated into his cardiac rehabilitation programme. (3) Set return appointment in 2–4 weeks to assess response. (4) Screen for suicidality (PHQ-9 item 9). (5) Involve the wife as a support — she has already identified the problem. Also reassess his cardiac rehabilitation engagement: "Have you been coming to the rehabilitation sessions?" Post-MI CR attendance in depressed patients is lower — active facilitation is needed. His secondary prevention medications are at target, which is excellent — now address the mental health component that will determine long-term adherence and quality of life.
